chunks.content: WHAT IS ALREADY KNOWN ON THIS TOPIC Patients with dextro-transposition of the great arteries (d-TGA) undergoing arterial switch operation (ASO) often require late cardiovascular interventions and may develop complications, frequently attributed to residual anatomical lesions such as ventricular septal defect (VSD). WHAT THIS STUDY ADDS This is the first study to demonstrate that aortic coarctation (CoA)—not VSD—is the strongest anatomical predictor of late cardiovascular morbidity after ASO, including recurrent right ventricular outflow tract (RVOT) and left ventricular outflow tract interventions. HOW THIS STUDY MIGHT AFFECT RESEARCH, PRACTICE OR POLICY These findings support more tailored surgical strategies and structured long-term surveillance for patients with d-TGA with CoA. Regular imaging and blood pressure monitoring are essential. Further research into the mechanisms linking CoA to RVOT morbidity is warranted. Introduction Dextro-transposition of the great arteries (d-TGA) accounts for 3% of congenital heart defects and 20% of cyanotic lesions. Without surgery, neonatal survival is rare. Since the late 1980s, the arterial switch operation (ASO) has been the standard treatment due to its low perioperative mortality and excellent outcomes, restoring physiological ventriculoarterial circulation. Young adults with ASO history form a growing adult congenital heart disease (ACHD) cohort, often with residual lesions that increase cardiovascular morbidity. Patients with d-TGA and complex cardiac anatomy are particularly at risk. However, even if among patients with d-TGA a complex cardiac anatomy is often defended by the presence of a concomitant ventricular septal defect (VSD), many authors also consider other associated lesions (such as aortic coarctation (CoA)) for purposes of classification. Therefore, definitions of anatomical cardiac complexity vary through literature, and the role of CoA in post-ASO morbidity is not well understood. Given the increased cardiovascular burden of patients with isolated CoA, this lesion may independently contribute to late cardiovascular morbidity if associated with d-TGA. This study aims to evaluate the impact of CoA, beyond VSD presence, on post-ASO interventions and cardiovascular complications. Methods Study design and patient population This prospective multicentre European registry was an initiative of the European collaboration for Prospective Outcome research in Congenital Heart disease (EPOCH, https://www.sacher-registry.com/epoch/ ). The EPOCH-ASO study is a prospective, multicentre cohort study of adults who underwent ASO, conducted by the EPOCH consortium. The study followed ethical guidelines, received approval from local and coordinating ethics committees, and all participants gave informed consent. Registered at ClinicalTrials.gov ( NCT04335448 ), it enrolled patients aged ≥16 with d-TGA or Taussig-Bing anomaly who had an ASO, a biventricular circulation and were followed at participating centres. The inclusion period ranged from October 2019 to June 2022. Exclusion criteria included inability to consent and prior heart transplant. Baseline data (demographics, cardiac anatomy, medical history, functional status, physical examination and blood tests) were collected by chart review. Cardiac imaging (echocardiography, cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR)) and cardiopulmonary exercise testing (CEPT) followed standardised protocols for consistency. Participants are being prospectively followed as per current guidelines for adults with congenital heart disease. Cardiac anatomy was categorised as simple (d-TGA with intact ventricular septum) or complex (d-TGA with VSD). For this analysis, 502 of 526 patients with available cardiac anatomy data were included. Left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) was assessed by transthoracic echocardiography, while right ventricular ejection fraction (RVEF) was assessed by CMR. Definitions The following were considered lesions associated with the right ventricular outflow tract (RVOT): pulmonary artery (PA) stenosis, neopulmonary valve stenosis/regurgitation and subvalvular pulmonary stenosis. Associated left ventricular outflow tract (LVOT) lesions included: CoA, aortic arch hypoplasia (diffuse narrowing of the aortic arch distal to the ascending aorta), bicuspid neoaortic valve and neoaortic valve stenosis/regurgitation. Shunt lesions included: atrial septal defects (ASDs), sinus venosus defects and patent arterial duct. An atrial septostomy performed before the ASO was considered as palliation. Post-ASO interventions included procedures related to the LVOT, the RVOT, percutaneous ablation procedure for arrhythmia, cardiac-device-related interventions and interventions related to the coronary arteries. RVOT-related interventions involved subvalvular pulmonary stenosis, neopulmonary valve valvuloplasty/replacement and PA interventions. LVOT-related interventions included subvalvular aortic stenosis resection, neoaortic valve procedures, aortic arch interventions and replacement of the neoaortic sinus/ascending aorta. ‘Other’ interventions included ASD/VSD closure beyond the first year of age, mitral valve-related interventions and occlusion of systemic-to-pulmonary collateral arteries. One intervention may have included multiple procedures (eg, balloon dilatation and stenting). Cardiovascular complications included heart failure, infective endocarditis, pulmonary hypertension, atrioventricular block III°, clinically relevant sustained arrhythmias, myocardial infarction and stroke (ischaemic and haemorrhagic), as defined by current guidelines. Heart failure occurring in the perinatal/perioperative period was not accounted as a cardiovascular complication. Study outcomes The primary outcome was time to the first post-ASO RVOT-related intervention, as these were the most common. Secondary outcomes included time to first LVOT-related intervention, time to first cardiovascular complication and the probability of event recurrence for RVOT-related and LVOT-related interventions at each time point. Statistical considerations Baseline patient characteristics were stratified by cardiac anatomy (complex vs simple).

included heart failure, infective endocarditis, pulmonary hypertension, atrioventricular block III°, clinically relevant sustained arrhythmias, myocardial infarction and stroke (ischaemic and haemorrhagic), as defined by current guidelines. Heart failure occurring in the perinatal/perioperative period was not accounted as a cardiovascular complication. Study outcomes The primary outcome was time to the first post-ASO RVOT-related intervention, as these were the most common. Secondary outcomes included time to first LVOT-related intervention, time to first cardiovascular complication and the probability of event recurrence for RVOT-related and LVOT-related interventions at each time point. Statistical considerations Baseline patient characteristics were stratified by cardiac anatomy (complex vs simple). Continuous variables were tested with the Shapiro-Wilk test, reported as median (IQR) and compared using Mann-Whitney U tests. Categorical variables were shown as counts (percentages) and compared using χ² or Fisher’s exact tests. Primary outcomes for complex versus simple anatomy and CoA versus non-CoA were analysed using Kaplan-Meier estimators, with event time from ASO to first event. Group differences were tested with log-rank tests, and HRs (95% CI) were estimated using Cox regression adjusted for anatomy, CoA, age at ASO and sex. Patients without events were censored at last recorded follow-up. Recurrent RVOT-related/LVOT-related interventions were analysed using event and mean cumulative function (MCF) plots, stratified by cardiac anatomy and CoA status. Groups were compared using two-sample pseudo-score tests. Multivariable Andersen-Gill models assessed the association of complex anatomy and CoA with recurrent intervention hazard, using robust standard errors. All tests were two-tailed; p<0.05 was considered statistically significant. Missing values in regression models were treated as missing and detailed in tables. Analyses were performed in R V.4.4.0 (R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria). Patient and public involvement statement Patients or the public were not involved in the design, or conduct, or reporting, or dissemination plans of our research. Results Patient characteristics at inclusion in the registry Patient characteristics at inclusion in the registry stratified by cardiac anatomy are shown in . Median age (IQR) was 25.5 (21.4–28.8) years, 31% were female and median BMI was 23.0 (20.9–26.0). 90% were in New York Heart Association class I, and 50% had a palliation. Patients with complex cardiac anatomy underwent ASO later than those with simple anatomy (16 (7–62) vs 8 (5–12) days, p<0.001). Associated lesions, particularly CoA (14% vs 2.2%, p<0.001), were more common in complex cases, except for coronary anomalies, which were similar between groups. Median age at ASO was higher in patients with CoA (21 (10–260) days) compared with those without CoA (8 (5–13.2) days), p<0.001. RVOT-related interventions occurred in 27% of the patients, while LVOT-related interventions occurred in 8.4%. Recurrent RVOT-related and LVOT-related interventions were frequent. LVOT-related interventions were more common in patients with complex cardiac anatomy (17% vs 4.8%, p<0.001), but RVOT interventions were equally distributed. Cardiovascular complications were more frequent in complex cardiac anatomy (26% vs 12%, p=0.002), driven by infective endocarditis and arrhythmia. LVEF and RVEF were normal. Peak oxygen uptake was equally reduced in both groups. Four patients with CoA had hypoplastic aortic arches, three of whom had an associated VSD. Of these four patients, two required post-ASO LVOT-related interventions (one patient without VSD underwent surgical repair of the aortic arch, while another patient with VSD required two CoA repairs via resection and end-to-end anastomosis at 0 and 10 years post-ASO). Additionally, three of them (two with VSD and one without) required at least one post-ASO RVOT-related intervention. Aortic root diameters were larger in patients with CoA than in those without (mean (IQR) 42 (39–47) vs 37 (33–41) mm, p<0.001) ( ). Moreover, antihypertensive treatment was more frequently required in the CoA group (49 (10.4%) vs 16 (55.2%)) ( ). Age at first post-ASO cardiovascular intervention/complication shows the number and median (IQR) age at first post-ASO cardiovascular intervention/complication. Post-ASO, 43% of patients underwent at least one intervention, and 18% experienced at least one cardiovascular complication . Median age (IQR) for RVOT-related reinterventions was 9.5 (3.8–15) years (supravalvular) and 16.4 (10.8–20.9) years (valvular). For LVOT reinterventions, median age was 12.7 (3.9–20.9) years (supravalvular) and 15.5 (6.9–23.3) years (valvular). Myocardial infarction, stroke and pulmonary hypertension occurred in early childhood, while infective endocarditis, heart failure and arrhythmia emerged in early adulthood. RVOT-related interventions were most frequent in childhood, whereas pacemaker (PM)-related interventions, coronary artery interventions, LVOT-related interventions and percutaneous ablation procedures for arrhythmia were common in adolescence and early adulthood. Flow of recurrent RVOT-related and LVOT-related interventions stratified by anatomical level Alluvial plots stratified by the presence or absence of CoA show the flow of RVOT-related and LVOT-related interventions by anatomical level and intervention number in . There were 242 RVOT-related interventions among 136 patients and 56 LVOT-related interventions among 42 patients. Most interventions occurred at the supravalvular level (86% RVOT, 48% LVOT). For RVOT-related interventions, this was consistent in patients with and without CoA. As expected, in patients

pacemaker (PM)-related interventions, coronary artery interventions, LVOT-related interventions and percutaneous ablation procedures for arrhythmia were common in adolescence and early adulthood. Flow of recurrent RVOT-related and LVOT-related interventions stratified by anatomical level Alluvial plots stratified by the presence or absence of CoA show the flow of RVOT-related and LVOT-related interventions by anatomical level and intervention number in . There were 242 RVOT-related interventions among 136 patients and 56 LVOT-related interventions among 42 patients. Most interventions occurred at the supravalvular level (86% RVOT, 48% LVOT). For RVOT-related interventions, this was consistent in patients with and without CoA. As expected, in patients with CoA, LVOT-related interventions were primarily supravalvular (76%). In contrast, in the absence of CoA, LVOT interventions were mainly valvular (49%). Number of RVOT-related and LVOT-related interventions by anatomical level and intervention details is depicted in . Supravalvular RVOT interventions were mainly percutaneous balloon angioplasties, while LVOT interventions were primarily mechanical aortic valve replacements and percutaneous interventions for CoA and re-CoA. shows a timeline of LVOT-related and RVOT-related interventions by anatomical level (y=age in years, x=patients). Rates of RVOT-related and LVOT-related interventions and cardiovascular complications stratified by CoA status depicts rates of post-ASO cardiovascular interventions and complications stratified by CoA status (yes vs no). Patients with concomitant CoA had higher rates of interventions related to the RVOT (51.7% vs 25.6%, p=0.004) and the LVOT (55.2% vs 5.5%, p<0.001) and of cardiovascular complications (41.4 vs 16.3%, p=0.001) than those without CoA. depicts the flow of patients with versus without RVOT-related/LVOT-related interventions and cardiovascular complications across sex, anatomical complexity (simple vs complex) and CoA status (yes vs no). Time to first RVOT-related/LVOT-related intervention and cardiovascular complications Kaplan-Meier curves comparing cumulative event rates of RVOT-related and LVOT-related interventions, and cardiovascular complications, are shown in . At a median follow-up of 25.5 (21.4–28.8] years, LVOT-related interventions and cardiovascular complications were higher in patients with a complex anatomy. Differences between patients with CoA and non-CoA were more pronounced in favour of patients with CoA. This was also true for cumulative event rates of RVOT-related interventions. Univariable HRs for post-ASO LVOT and RVOT interventions are depicted in . Multivariable-adjusted HRs for post-ASO interventions and cardiovascular complications at a median age of 25.5 (21.4–28.8) years are shown in . Complex cardiac anatomy was associated with increased risk of LVOT-related interventions (HR (95% CI) 2.11 (1.04 to 4.28)) and cardiovascular complications (HR (95% CI) 1.78 (1.14 to 2.79)); CoA was associated with increased risk of LVOT-related interventions (HR (95% CI) 10.75 (5.12 to 22.57)) and cardiovascular complications (HR (95% CI) 2.16 (1.12 to 4.18)). Only CoA predicted RVOT-related interventions (HR (95% CI) 2.62 (1.47 to 4.68)). Analysis of recurrent events A comparison of recurrence rate probabilities for RVOT-related and LVOT-related interventions for simple versus complex cardiac anatomy and CoA versus no CoA is depicted in . The MCF plots depict the estimation of the probability of event recurrence at each time point (continuous lines) and their 95% CI (dotted lines). The probability of LVOT-related intervention recurrence over time was higher among patients with complex cardiac anatomy compared with those with simple anatomy, as well as among patients with CoA compared with those without. However, only having CoA was associated with a higher probability of RVOT-related intervention recurrence. In multivariable Andersen-Gill models accounting for recurrent events, CoA was strongly associated with increased hazard of LVOT reinterventions (HR 8.16, 95% CI 3.72 to 17.87, p<0.001) and RVOT reinterventions (HR 2.15, 95% CI 1.34 to 3.45, p=0.001). Complex anatomy was associated with a higher hazard of LVOT reintervention (HR 2.64, 95% CI 1.19 to 5.87, p=0.017), but not with RVOT reintervention (p=0.81). Event plots ( ) depict the timing of recurrent events (each green dot represents a single event) for individual subjects (each grey bar is a single patient) across the study period (years since ASO until the baseline study visit). Discussion This study is the first to analyse the impact of CoA beyond anatomical cardiac complexity defined by the presence or absence of VSD on post-ASO cardiovascular interventions and complications. We also uniquely examine predictors for recurrent interventions involving the LVOT and RVOT. Cardiovascular interventions post-ASO were common, especially those related to the LVOT and RVOT interventions. A concomitant CoA, not a VSD, showed the highest HR for LVOT-related and RVOT-related interventions and cardiovascular complications. The probability of intervention recurrence over time was higher in patients with CoA. Our findings compared with the current literature Post-ASO interventions related to the RVOT Supravalvular pulmonary stenosis is a key midterm complication in children after ASO. This, along with RVOT-related reinterventions, often reduces exercise capacity, a key predictor of long-term morbidity. The lower values observed in our study, as well as in other reports, compared with those described by Kempny et al , may partly reflect age-related differences, as this last cohort included

not a VSD, showed the highest HR for LVOT-related and RVOT-related interventions and cardiovascular complications. The probability of intervention recurrence over time was higher in patients with CoA. Our findings compared with the current literature Post-ASO interventions related to the RVOT Supravalvular pulmonary stenosis is a key midterm complication in children after ASO. This, along with RVOT-related reinterventions, often reduces exercise capacity, a key predictor of long-term morbidity. The lower values observed in our study, as well as in other reports, compared with those described by Kempny et al , may partly reflect age-related differences, as this last cohort included younger patients. Despite surgical and percutaneous interventions, residual RVOT obstruction remains common in patients with d-TGA long after the ASO. In this study, RVOT-related interventions after ASO were frequent (27%), primarily at a supravalvular level. Unlike previous findings, the presence of a concomitant VSD was not linked to an increased risk for RVOT-related interventions. Instead, CoA emerged as the main risk factor for interventions at this level. Given the higher prevalence of CoA among patients with complex anatomy (14% vs 2.2%, p<0.001), VSD may act as a surrogate marker of risk when associated with CoA. The combination of VSD and CoA may be related to an anterior deviation of the conal septum, resulting in limited antegrade flow across the aortic valve during fetal life. However, RVOT interventions were equally prevalent among patients with and without VSD (27% each), and 89% of first RVOT interventions occurred in patients without CoA, suggesting that post-ASO anatomical factors (such as PA overstretching or compression between the sternum and neoaortic root) may be major contributors. Importantly, patients with CoA often present additional lesions such as aortic root hypoplasia, ascending aortic dilatation and a bicuspid aortic valve (BAV). More than half of patients with CoA (up to 75% in some reports) have an associated BAV, and those with both CoA and BAV have been shown to carry a fourfold increased risk of aortic valve and ascending aortic interventions compared with patients with a trileaflet valve. Building on these observations, we postulate that associated lesions commonly observed in CoA—particularly aortic root hypoplasia, ascending aortic dilation and potentially stenotic bicuspid neopulmonic valves—may exacerbate post-ASO anatomical vulnerabilities, leading to RVOT-related obstructions and reinterventions. Specifically, a stenotic bicuspid neopulmonic valve, compression of the PA by a dilated ascending aorta or neo-PA root hypoplasia could act as primary drivers of later interventions in this population. Although a bicuspid neopulmonary valve remains a plausible contributor to RVOT stenosis and reintervention, its detailed morphological assessment was not feasible in our cohort due to technical limitations. The anterior and retrosternal positioning of the RVOT, combined with valve stretching after the LeCompte manoeuvre, often hampers visualisation even with advanced imaging. In our cohort, patients with CoA exhibited larger aortic root diameters and more frequent use of antihypertensive therapy ( ), suggesting a shared underlying aortopathy influenced by hypertension through progressive aortic dilatation and exacerbation of anatomical vulnerabilities. Therefore, in addition to regular blood pressure monitoring, cardiopulmonary exercise testing every 3–5 years (to detect hypertensive responses) and periodic 24-hour ambulatory monitoring (if masked hypertension is suspected) should be performed in ASO patients with CoA. Cross-sectional imaging of the aortic root, ascending aorta and arch should also be conducted every 3–5 years, tailored to the degree of dilation and clinical risk. Post-ASO interventions related to the LVOT Left-sided cardiac lesions, such as neoaortic valve regurgitation or recoarctation, are frequently observed in patients with d-TGA after ASO. In our study, interventions related to these lesions were less frequent than RVOT-related interventions. However, since they often occur later in life, their prevalence may increase over time due to progressive recoarctations or prosthetic valve complications. As expected, patients with CoA were at the highest risk for LVOT-related interventions, mainly driven by recoarctation procedures. Mohammadi et al reported that higher aortic root/ascending aorta ratios are associated with recoarctation in patients with d-TGA with VSD and CoA. Turbulent flow in the neoaorta, attributed to aortic arch angulation from the LeCompte manoeuvre, may further exacerbate this risk, especially when PA mobilisation is insufficient. In CoA cases, an enlarged neoaortic root combined with a smaller distal aorta intensifies blood turbulence, promoting aortic valve regurgitation and recoarctation. Preventing these complications may require meticulous VSD closure and balanced aortic reconstruction. Age at RVOT-related and LVOT-related interventions for the different anatomical levels We hypothesise that the earlier occurrence of RVOT-related interventions compared with LVOT-related ones results from ASO-related factors, such as PA overstretching after the LeCompte manoeuvre, and, in patients with CoA, additional anatomical features like a stenotic bicuspid neopulmonic valve or neo-PA root hypoplasia. Supravalvular RVOT interventions typically occur at younger ages than valvular interventions. Longer follow-up may reveal progressive neoaortic root dilation leading to neoaortic valve regurgitation, or growth-related proximal RVOT compression requiring neoaortic valve

and recoarctation. Preventing these complications may require meticulous VSD closure and balanced aortic reconstruction. Age at RVOT-related and LVOT-related interventions for the different anatomical levels We hypothesise that the earlier occurrence of RVOT-related interventions compared with LVOT-related ones results from ASO-related factors, such as PA overstretching after the LeCompte manoeuvre, and, in patients with CoA, additional anatomical features like a stenotic bicuspid neopulmonic valve or neo-PA root hypoplasia. Supravalvular RVOT interventions typically occur at younger ages than valvular interventions. Longer follow-up may reveal progressive neoaortic root dilation leading to neoaortic valve regurgitation, or growth-related proximal RVOT compression requiring neoaortic valve replacement, RVOT augmentation and neopulmonary valve replacement. Post-ASO cardiovascular complications Cardiovascular complications were more common in patients with CoA, driven by higher rates of arrhythmias and infective endocarditis. While complex cardiac anatomy has been linked to complications in ASO patients, it was no longer a risk factor after adjusting for CoA, suggesting CoA is the primary predictor, particularly for arrhythmias and infective endocarditis. Infective endocarditis, though rare (1.6% in our cohort), was more prevalent in patients with CoA, as well as arrhythmia, consistent with prior studies. Higher arrhythmia rates may be linked to arterial hypertension and myocardial hypertrophy, as CoA patients in our study were more often on antihypertensive treatment. Mejis et al , showed that endocarditis was linked to aortic valve prostheses. In our cohort, prostheses were more common in patients without CoA. Therefore, the higher rates of infective endocarditis in patients with CoA might be related to other factors, such as residual VSD, though further data are needed to confirm this. Limitations As the registry includes only adult ASO survivors, a survival bias is present, potentially skewing time-based estimates by excluding those with more severe disease. Nonetheless, the findings are valid for patients followed in ACHD clinics. Although the analysis was prospective, data inclusion was retrospective, limiting causal inference; thus, the evidence is hypothesis-generating. CoA prevalence was low (6%), and first RVOT-related interventions among patients with CoA accounted for 11% of cases, leaving risk factors among non-CoA patients to be elucidated. Due to the low number of events, predictors for PM-related, coronary or ablation interventions and their functional impact were not analysed. Moreover, the absence of CMR or CT data on great artery diameters and flow velocities limits further mechanistic insights. Finally, the lack of detailed information on concomitant procedures (eg, VSD repair, vessel augmentation) hampers understanding of how anatomical complexity affects outcomes. Conclusion Patients with d-TGA and CoA face the highest risk of recurrent RVOT-related/LVOT-related interventions and cardiovascular complications after ASO. While the higher LVOT intervention rates in patients with CoA are expected, the mechanisms behind the increased risk for RVOT-related interventions and cardiovascular morbidity in these patients remain unclear. As RVOT interventions are the most common post-ASO procedures, these findings are clinically relevant. Special attention should be given to patients with d-TGA and CoA both at the moment of repair in order to prevent future RVOT obstruction, and during their life-long follow-up, which should include structured cardiovascular imaging and blood pressure monitoring. chunks.content: 1 Introduction Cervical cancer is the fourth most prevalent malignancy in women and remains a significant global health burden, with population‐based data indicating an overall 5‐year survival approaching 70% [ ]. Stage‐dependent survival varied markedly among cervical cancer patients from 2000 to 2021. Patients with early‐stage disease (FIGO IA) had a favorable prognosis, with a 5‐year overall survival of 95.3%, whereas those with advanced‐stage disease (FIGO IV) experienced substantially poorer survival, at only 18.1% [ ]. Despite notable progress achieved through vaccination and early screening programs, which have greatly reduced incidence in many regions, the disease still exerts substantial morbidity and mortality in developing and low‐income countries where medical resources remain limited [ , ]. Cisplatin (DDP) is widely regarded as the cornerstone and first‐line chemotherapeutic drug in cervical cancer treatment [ ]. Although patients often exhibit an initial favorable response, prolonged exposure to cisplatin frequently results in acquired resistance, driving tumor recurrence and metastasis and ultimately compromising overall prognosis [ , ]. Consequently, developing innovative therapeutic options to address the issue of cisplatin resistance or enhance cisplatin chemosensitivity has become an urgent clinical priority. Multiple molecular events have been known to participate in cisplatin resistance, including enhanced DNA damage repair capacity, impaired apoptosis signaling, and aberrant redox homeostasis, and so forth [ , ]. Recently, lipid metabolism, particularly cholesterol metabolism, has been reported to emerge as a crucial metabolic determinant of tumor chemoresistance [ ]. Cholesterol is indispensable for maintaining membrane structure, receptor activity, and signal transduction [ ]. Elevated cholesterol levels in cancer cells may accelerate proliferation, suppress apoptosis, and even promote resistance to chemotherapy [ ]. Statins, compounds targeting HMG‐CoA reductase, have long been used as lipid‐lowering medications and are recognized for their favorable safety profile [ ]. Based on lipophilicity, a property to penetrate cell membranes and tissues, statins are typically classified into lipophilic statins and hydrophilic statins [ ]. Lipophilic statins have higher membrane permeability, broader cellular uptake and enhanced anti‐tumor activity compared with hydrophilic statins, and have been associated with reduced all‐cause and cancer‐specific mortality [ , , ]. Beyond their cardiovascular applications, accumulating evidence suggests that statins possess anticancer potential and can potentiate the efficacy of conventional chemotherapeutics in several tumor types [ ]. A recent meta‐analysis across multiple cancer types found that statin therapy was associated with improved survival in advanced‐stage malignancies [ ]. Accumulating epidemiological evidence suggests a protective role of statins against cervical cancer. Specifically, the use of statins for at least 6 months has been associated with a reduced risk of cervical cancer incidence, lower mortality, and improved survival outcomes [ , ]. However, the influence of statins on cisplatin resistance and the molecular mechanism underlying this effect in cervical cancer remains largely unexplored. Caveolin‐1 (CAV1), a scaffold protein localized within cholesterol‐rich caveolae microdomains, coordinates numerous processes such as signal organization, molecular trafficking, and cholesterol homeostasis [ ]. Cholesterol depletion induced by statins affects caveolae organization, where CAV1 functions as a structural scaffold [ ]. Aberrant CAV1 expression has been reported to reinforce the function and stability of ATP‐binding cassette transporters, leading to enhanced drug efflux and reduced intracellular drug concentration [ ]. Meanwhile, the PI3K/AKT pathway, composed of phosphoinositide 3‐kinase and protein kinase B, is a critical signaling axis regulating cell survival and proliferation and has been reported to be influenced by CAV1 in an expression‐dependent manner [ , ]. Dysregulated activation or mutation within this pathway is frequently associated with tumor development and anticancer agent resistance [ ]. Despite these insights, whether modulating CAV1 expression can influence the PI3K/AKT axis and consequently resensitize cisplatin‐resistant cervical cancer cells has not yet been determined. Herein, cisplatin‐resistant cervical cancer cell lines were established to explore their cholesterol metabolism and statins' responsiveness compared with those of their parental counterparts. The combinatorial antitumor efficacy of simvastatin and cisplatin both in vitro and in vivo was further evaluated. Mechanistic investigations involved CAV1 knockdown to assess its role in chemosensitivity and western blot analyses to monitor alterations in CAV1 expression and PI3K/AKT pathway activation following individual or combined treatments. Collectively, this work provides new experimental evidence that simvastatin targeting the CAV1/PI3K/AKT signaling axis may represent a promising strategy to counteract cisplatin resistance in cervical cancer. 2 Materials and Methods 2.1 Cell Culture and Establishment of Cisplatin‐Resistant Cervical Cancer Cell Lines SiHa and C33a, two human cervical cancer cell lines, and 293T cells were obtained from the American Type Culture Collection (ATCC, USA). Cisplatin‐resistant cervical cancer cells (SiHa‐DDP and C33a‐DDP) were constructed from SiHa and C33a cells. Dulbecco's modified Eagle's medium (DMEM; Meilunbio, China) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS; Sunrise, Uruguay) and 1% penicillin–streptomycin (100 mg/mL; Invitrogen, UK) was employed to culture cells at 37°C in a humidified 5% CO 2 atmosphere. SiHa‐DDP and C33a‐DDP cells were generated by gradually treating the parental

cancer. 2 Materials and Methods 2.1 Cell Culture and Establishment of Cisplatin‐Resistant Cervical Cancer Cell Lines SiHa and C33a, two human cervical cancer cell lines, and 293T cells were obtained from the American Type Culture Collection (ATCC, USA). Cisplatin‐resistant cervical cancer cells (SiHa‐DDP and C33a‐DDP) were constructed from SiHa and C33a cells. Dulbecco's modified Eagle's medium (DMEM; Meilunbio, China) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS; Sunrise, Uruguay) and 1% penicillin–streptomycin (100 mg/mL; Invitrogen, UK) was employed to culture cells at 37°C in a humidified 5% CO 2 atmosphere. SiHa‐DDP and C33a‐DDP cells were generated by gradually treating the parental SiHa and C33a cells with escalating doses of cisplatin over several months. The cisplatin concentration was gradually increased in a stepwise manner (0.5, 1, 2, 4, 6, 10 μM) to select resistant populations. Increasing evidence implicates dysregulated cholesterol metabolism as a critical contributor to the development of drug resistance. In hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), elevated cholesterol levels remodeled lipid rafts to activate oncogenic signaling pathways [ ]. Sorafenib‐resistant HCC cells displayed increased intracellular cholesterol, and cholesterol reduction restored sorafenib sensitivity [ ]. Likewise, in non‐small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), gefitinib‐resistant cells exhibited higher lipid‐raft cholesterol content than their sensitive counterparts, and cholesterol depletion enhanced gefitinib efficacy [ , ]. Moreover, recent studies targeting cholesterol synthesis or uptake have demonstrated that inhibition of cholesterol metabolism could overcome platinum‐based drug resistance. Wang et al. [ ] reported that the reduction of intracellular cholesterol markedly alleviated cisplatin resistance in breast cancer cells. They developed platinum (IV) complexes FP (fenofibrate‐platinum [IV]) and DFP (difluorofenofibrate‐platinum [IV]), which effectively overcame cisplatin resistance by inhibiting cholesterol metabolism in addition to inducing DNA damage. Squalene epoxidase (SQLE), an enzyme involved in cholesterol biosynthesis, has been shown to promote chemoresistance via cholesterol‐dependent AKT activation in head and neck cancers [ ]. In the present study, SiHa‐DDP and C33a‐DDP, two cervical cancer cell lines exhibiting resistance to cisplatin, were successfully established to simulate clinical drug resistance. Compared with their parental counterparts, the resistant variants exhibited significantly elevated intracellular cholesterol levels, suggesting that dysregulated cholesterol metabolism may contribute to cisplatin resistance. After evaluating the cytotoxicity of seven statins approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA), both parental and cisplatin‐resistant cervical cancer cells displayed increased sensitivity to lipophilic statins, which may be attributed to their higher membrane permeability, facilitating intracellular accumulation. However, cisplatin‐resistant cells displayed relative tolerance to these agents, implying that cisplatin resistance may be accompanied by adaptive changes in cholesterol metabolism that confer a broader multidrug‐resistant phenotype. Statins, as inhibitors of HMGCR, primarily block de novo cholesterol biosynthesis [ ]. Increasing evidence supports that statins not only exerted antitumor effects beyond lipid regulation but also enhanced the chemosensitivity of tumor cells [ ]. [ ] used experimental evidence obtained from both cell‐based systems and animal models, which indicated that pitavastatin directly bound to neuropilin‐1 (NRP1) and was shown to reverse resistance to cisplatin in both colorectal carcinoma and non‐small‐cell lung cancer. As for the present study, simvastatin, the most lipophilic statin, co‐treatment with cisplatin yielded a significant synergistic response in cervical cancer cells exhibiting cisplatin resistance. Compared with either drug alone, the combination treatment significantly enhanced apoptosis and suppressed cell migration. Additionally, in vivo experiments demonstrated that co‐treatment with simvastatin and cisplatin significantly suppressed tumor growth in cisplatin‐resistant cervical cancer models. Simvastatin was administered at 30 mg/kg every 2 days, a dose derived from FDA‐approved clinical regimens (20–40 mg/day, with a maximum of 80 mg/day) using body surface area conversion [ ]. This dose falls within the range commonly applied in preclinical studies and accounts for interspecies differences in pharmacokinetics and oral bioavailability. Previous studies have employed comparable dosing regimens to evaluate the antitumor effects of simvastatin [ ]. HE staining of major organs revealed no obvious histological toxicity. Together, these findings indicate that the dosing strategy is scientifically justified and clinically informative, highlighting the potential of simvastatin as an adjunct therapy in cisplatin‐resistant cervical cancer. All the results indicated that simvastatin potentiated cisplatin efficacy and might represent a new approach for treating cisplatin resistance in resistant cervical cancer cells. Caveolin‐1, the principal structural component of lipid rafts, plays a critical role in regulating membrane fluidity and cholesterol metabolism [ ]. There are various studies demonstrating the association between overexpression of CAV1 and chemoresistance in cancers, such as hepatocellular carcinoma [ ], pancreatic cancer [ ], and melanoma [ ]. Pereira et al. [ ] demonstrated high CAV1 protein levels reduced HER2 membrane availability, thereby limiting antibody‐drug conjugates (ADCs) binding and internalization in heterogeneous gastric cancer. What's more, CAV1 overexpression has also been shown to suppress cisplatin‐induced apoptosis and promote cell survival in gastric cancer through stimulation of the WNT signaling cascade via LRP6 phosphorylation and β‐catenin dephosphorylation [ ]. Besides, it was the first to establish CAV1‐knockdown cisplatin‐resistant cervical cancer cell lines, demonstrating that CAV1 suppression markedly increased cisplatin sensitivity. Therefore, it was suggested that CAV1 represented a promising target for overcoming cisplatin resistance. Moreover, both simvastatin monotherapy and its combination with cisplatin significantly reduced CAV1 expression in resistant cervical cancer cells, with the combination showing a more pronounced effect. These results indicated that simvastatin might enhance the cisplatin sensitivity of cervical cancer cells resistant to cisplatin by downregulating CAV1 and disrupting lipid raft‐associated signaling. Nowadays, activation of the PI3K/AKT signaling cascade is recognized as a crucial mechanism underlying reduced chemosensitivity [ ]. Histone lysine crotonylation (Kcr), regulated by acyl‐CoA synthetase short‐chain family member 2 (ACSS2), could activate the PI3K/AKT pathway and then drive EGFR‐TKI resistance in lung cancer [ ]. [ ] showed that cisplatin induced CCL5 secretion from senescent cancer‐associated fibroblasts (CAFs) in neuroendocrine prostate cancer, which activated the CCR5/PI3K/AKT pathway in tumor cells to promote DNA repair and resistance. And Zhu et al. [ ] reported that simvastatin overcame ferroptosis and chemo‐immunotherapy resistance in AKT‐hyperactivated intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma. The present study carried out a western blot assay to detect PI3K, AKT, and p‐AKT protein levels. It was found that PI3K and p‐AKT were reduced in simvastatin and simvastatin combined with cisplatin groups, demonstrating that simvastatin significantly suppressed the PI3K/AKT signaling pathway activation. Besides, to further investigate whether simvastatin exerted its effect by suppressing the expression of CAV1 and subsequently regulating the activation of the PI3K/AKT signaling pathway, a rescue experiment was performed in cisplatin‐resistant cervical cancer cells with CAV1 overexpression. It was found that PI3K and p‐AKT were reduced in simvastatin and simvastatin combined with cisplatin groups, demonstrating that simvastatin significantly suppressed the PI3K/AKT signaling pathway activation. Besides, to further investigate whether simvastatin exerted its effect by suppressing the expression of CAV1 and subsequently regulating the activation of the PI3K/AKT signaling pathway, a rescue experiment was performed in cisplatin‐resistant cervical cancer cells with CAV1 overexpression. These findings suggested that simvastatin might enhance cisplatin sensitivity by inhibiting CAV1 expression, thereby attenuating the PI3K/AKT signaling pathway activation. Several limitations of the present study should be acknowledged. Although cholesterol accumulation was observed in resistant cells, the underlying metabolic mechanisms were not dissected and warrant further investigation. And the experimental design for repeated in vivo studies and survival analyses will be incorporated into future investigations. Transcriptome‐wide profiling in statin‐treated models may provide deeper insight into molecular alterations associated with cisplatin resistance. 5 Conclusion In conclusion, our study demonstrated that simvastatin combined with cisplatin exerted a synergistic anticancer effect in cervical cancer cells which were resistant to cisplatin, as shown both in vitro and in vivo. Mechanistically, simvastatin downregulated CAV1 expression, thereby attenuating the activation of the PI3K/AKT signaling pathway. These findings identified a novel pathway by which simvastatin functions as a potential co‐therapy to potentiate the impact of cisplatin treatment on cervical cancer cells. chunks.content: 1 Introduction Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is the leading cause of death worldwide, accounting for nearly 40% of deaths among individuals over 65 years of age ( ). Its burden has risen dramatically over recent decades, with global prevalence nearly doubling between 1990 and 2019, increasing from 271 million to 523 million cases and resulting in 19.1 million deaths in 2020 ( ). This rise reflects complex interactions between demographic transitions, including population aging, lifestyle changes, accumulation of comorbidities, and medical advances, that while helpful, also heighten long-term cardiovascular health ( ). Importantly, epidemiologic data show that CVD incidence varies not only by age and sex, but also by menopausal status. According to the American Heart Association, nearly 40% of adults aged 40–59 years, 75% of those aged 60–79, and 86% of those over 80 are affected by some form of CVD ( ). Before menopause, men exhibit nearly threefold higher prevalence compared to women, but this gap narrows sharply after menopause, suggesting a cardiovascular-protective role of estrogen and its receptors ( ; ). These observations highlight the significance of estrogen signaling pathways in shaping sex-specific differences in CVD ( ; ; ). Pharmacological agents that influence estrogen pathways represent a particularly important factor in this context, with SERMs serving as a prominent example. Originally developed for reproductive and oncologic applications, SERMs have been widely prescribed for breast cancer prevention, osteoporosis treatment and other gynecologic conditions ( ). However, their effects extend beyond reproductive tissues, as they engage estrogen receptors (ERs) across metabolic and cardiovascular systems. This duality explains their capacity to produce beneficial outcomes, such as favorable modulation of lipid profiles and vascular tones, while simultaneously elevating thromboembolic risk under certain conditions ( ). Given these contrasting actions, therapeutic decisions regarding SERM use require careful balancing of reproductive benefits against cardiovascular implications. The following sections therefore first examine the physiology of estrogen and its receptors, establishing the foundation for understanding how SERMs modulate cardiovascular health. Accordingly, the central aim of this review is to critically examine how SERMs modulate vascular biology and cardiovascular risk through estrogen receptor–dependent mechanisms. Rather than positioning SERMs as primary cardioprotective therapies, this article specifically evaluates their molecular, cellular, and clinical vascular effects—highlighting both protective actions (e.g., endothelial function, lipid modulation) and adverse liabilities (e.g., thrombosis). By integrating mechanistic insights with evidence from major clinical trials, this review seeks to clarify why favorable surrogate vascular markers have not consistently translated into improved cardiovascular outcomes, and to define the implications of these findings for the future design and clinical use of next-generation estrogen receptor–targeted therapies. 2 Estrogen and cardiovascular health 2.1 Estrogen and its primary site of production Estrogens are a family of steroidal sex hormones that regulate reproductive organ function in both sexes, while also governing diverse systemic processes relevant to cardiovascular physiology ( ; ). Four major estrogens—estrone (E1), estradiol (E2), estriol (E3), and estretrol (E4)—exhibit distinct roles and secretion patterns across different physiological states. E1 predominates after menopause, while E3 and E4 are produced almost exclusively during pregnancy ( ; ). E2, also known as 17β-estradiol, is the most potent and biologically abundant estrogen in premenopausal women and is often considered the principal form in studies of cardiovascular regulation ( ; ; ). Because of its dominant role outside pregnancy, estradiol serves as the focal point for understanding estrogen-mediated cardiovascular effects. Estrogen is synthesized in both gonadal and extra-gonadal tissues, contributing to systemic and local effects across various organs ( ). In females of reproductive age, the ovaries constitute the primary site of estrogen production, with biosynthesis initiated in the theca cells and completed in granulosa cells through enzymatic conversion ( ; ). In males, the testes produce smaller quantities of estrogen, underscoring the hormone’s relevance beyond female reproduction ( ; ; ). Extra-gonadal sources, particularly adipose tissue, represent a significant source of estrogen for both sexes, becoming more prominent with age and increased fat mass ( ; ). Additional extra-gonadal sites of estrogen synthesis include bone, adrenal glands, skin, muscle, vascular endothelium, intestines, liver, and vascular smooth muscle. In these tissues, estrogen acts locally through paracrine or intracrine signaling rather than entering systemic circulation ( ; ; ). Such extra-gonadal activity becomes the predominant source of estrogen production in postmenopausal women and in men, highlighting its significance once ovarian and testicular output declines ( ; ). 2.2 Estrogen receptors and their location Estrogen exerts its multifaceted biological effects primarily through binding to well-characterized receptor subtypes located across various target tissues ( ). The estrogen receptor (ER) family comprises two canonical nuclear receptors, estrogen receptor-α (ERα) and estrogen receptor-β (ERβ) as well as the membrane-associated G-protein coupled receptor known as GPR30 (GPER1) ( ; ). Each contains distinct functional domains enabling DNA-binding, ligand-binding, and transcriptional activation ( ). Upon estrogen binding, Estrogen primarily acts

predominant source of estrogen production in postmenopausal women and in men, highlighting its significance once ovarian and testicular output declines ( ; ). 2.2 Estrogen receptors and their location Estrogen exerts its multifaceted biological effects primarily through binding to well-characterized receptor subtypes located across various target tissues ( ). The estrogen receptor (ER) family comprises two canonical nuclear receptors, estrogen receptor-α (ERα) and estrogen receptor-β (ERβ) as well as the membrane-associated G-protein coupled receptor known as GPR30 (GPER1) ( ; ). Each contains distinct functional domains enabling DNA-binding, ligand-binding, and transcriptional activation ( ). Upon estrogen binding, Estrogen primarily acts through two classical nuclear receptors. Once bound to these receptors, ERα and ERβ undergo conformational changes that facilitate dimerization and translocation to the nucleus, where they regulate gene expression via direct binding to estrogen response elements, or via modulating other transcription factors, thereby initiating the classical genomic pathways ( ; ). Complementing this, membrane-associated ERs and GPR30 mediate rapid non-genomic pathway. Estrogen engages membrane-associated ERα, ERβ, or GPR30, activating rapid signaling by activating intracellular kinase pathways, such as MAPK and PI3K, which influence gene expression and cellular responses within minutes ( ; ). This duality of genomic and non-genomic pathways enables estrogen to exert both immediate and sustained effects. The tissue-specific distribution of ERs critically shapes the hormone’s biological actions ( ). ERα is predominantly expressed in reproductive tissues, including the mammary glands, uterus, ovarian theca cells, as well as in the liver, adipose tissue, kidney, and bones ( ). Functionally, it drives reproductive development, metabolic, regulation, and skeletal maintenance ( ). In contrast, ERβ is more abundant in the prostate epithelium, ovarian granulosa cells, bone marrow, colon, immune cells and brain, often acting as a modulator by forming heterodimers with ERα to attenuate its transcriptional activity ( ). GPR30 is also widely expressed, particularly in reproductive organs, brain, adrenal glands, adipocytes, bone, kidney, and heart, whereby it mediates rapid, non-genomic signaling that influences vascular tone, glucose metabolism, and neuronal activity ( ; ). Within the cardiovascular system, both ERα and ERβ are expressed in cardiomyocytes, vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs), and endothelial cells, where they regulate nitric oxide (NO) production, vascular remodeling, and cardiac responses to hemodynamic stress ( ; ). Importantly, mechanisms of crosstalk between these signaling pathways converge on transcriptional regulation, whereby phosphorylation events mediated by GPR30-activated kinases enhance the transcriptional activity of nuclear receptors and associated transcription factors such as AP-1, STATs, and NF-κB ( ). This integrated signaling network allows estrogen to exert finely tuned, context-dependent effects essential for cardiovascular function and systemic endocrine balance ( ). Understanding these complex receptor mechanisms provides critical insights for therapeutic targeting of estrogen signaling in diverse diseases affecting reproductive, metabolic, and cardiovascular systems. Importantly, this heterogeneous distribution and signaling integration of ERα, ERβ, and GPR30 within the cardiovascular system establishes the mechanistic basis by which selective estrogen receptor modulation can yield divergent vascular outcomes—ranging from endothelial protection to maladaptive remodeling—depending on receptor subtype engagement, tissue context, and hormonal milieu. 2.3 Variation of Estrogen with gender, age and in relation to menopause Gender, age, and menopausal status are critical determinants of circulating estrogen levels and, consequently, have profound implications on cardiovascular health. In men, plasma estrogen concentrations remain relatively stable across adulthood, and begin to decline gradually after the age of 60 ( ). Contrastingly, premenopausal women exhibit significantly higher serum estrogen levels, generally ranging from 15 to 300 pg/mL during the reproductive years. However, following menopause, this concentration sharply declines to less than 15–40 pg/mL, resulting in postmenopausal estrogen levels comparable to those in age-matched men ( ; ; ). This sharp reduction in estrogen following menopause is associated with a markedly increased risk of CVD. Indeed, studies indicate a 4.3-fold higher incidence of CVD in postmenopausal women compared to men in the same age bracket ( ). In addition to reduced estrogen levels, menopause is associated with decreased expression and altered signaling of ERs, which further exacerbates cardiovascular vulnerability ( ). The expression of ERα, the principal receptor mediating estrogen’s effects in endothelial cells, declines by roughly 33% after menopause, compared to levels during the late follicular phase of the menstrual cycle ( ). This decline is largely attributed to reduced estrogen availability ( ). Aging also contributes to this decrease in ERα expression with transcriptional downregulation observed in aging tissues ( ). Notably, this effect appears sex specific as ERα expression remains stable in male murine models ( ). Therefore, these findings underscore that decreased estrogen availability plays a crucial role in influencing receptor expression, whereas aging may further modulate this process in a context-dependent and sex-specific manner. Collectively, the interplay of declining estrogen and receptor changes during menopause shapes cardiovascular outcomes and highlights the need for targeted interventions in this population. 2.4 Cardioprotective effect of

Notably, this effect appears sex specific as ERα expression remains stable in male murine models ( ). Therefore, these findings underscore that decreased estrogen availability plays a crucial role in influencing receptor expression, whereas aging may further modulate this process in a context-dependent and sex-specific manner. Collectively, the interplay of declining estrogen and receptor changes during menopause shapes cardiovascular outcomes and highlights the need for targeted interventions in this population. 2.4 Cardioprotective effect of Estrogen Gender significantly influences CVD prevalence, with premenopausal women exhibiting relative cardiovascular-protection compared to men—a notion largely attributed to estrogen and its receptors ( ). While extensive research has elucidated many estrogen-mediated cardiovascular benefits, the precise mechanisms by which specific ERs subtypes confer protection remain incompletely understood ( ; ). Estrogen exerts direct effects on cardiovascular system by promoting vasorelaxation, as well as enhancing proliferation and migration of vascular endothelial cells, thus facilitating vascular repair and health. In contrast, it suppresses proliferation and migration of VSMCs, thereby mitigating vascular remodeling. Estrogen also modulates cardiomyocyte function by improving insulin sensitivity, and protecting against myocardial infarction, cardiac hypertrophy, and ischemia–reperfusion injury through complex genomic and non-genomic signaling. A key component of estrogen’s cardioprotective action includes GPR30-mediated reduction in low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) transcytosis across endothelial cells, a crucial early event in atherogenesis ( ; ; ). This mechanism highlights a novel endothelial-specific pathway by which estrogen lowers LDL-C entry into vascular walls, further contributing to cardiovascular protection ( ). These multifaceted mechanisms collectively underpin the observed gender differences in CVD incidence during reproductive years, emphasizing estrogen’s pivotal role in cardiovascular protection. In addition to these direct actions, estrogen indirectly promotes cardiovascular health by modulating coagulation factors, reducing oxidative stress through decreased production of reactive oxygen species (ROS), and favorably influencing metabolic processes ( ). However, these beneficial effects decline with advancing age, particularly after the late postmenopausal phase (above 59 years), coinciding with increased cardiovascular risk ( ). This attenuation is linked to age-related alterations in ER expression and signaling efficiency, diminishing estrogen’s protective capacity ( ). Recognizing this critical transition is essential for developing targeted strategies to sustain cardiovascular health in aging women. 3 SERMs 3.1 Introducing SERMs SERMs are nonsteroidal compounds that exert estrogenic or antiestrogenic effects in a tissue-selective manner ( ). This dual functionality enables SERMs to act as agonists in some tissues while serving as antagonists in others, thereby expanding their clinical utility in managing postmenopausal osteoporosis, hormone-responsive cancers, and CVD ( ; ). Developed since 1960s, SERMs such as tamoxifen—the first to gain FDA approval—transformed the therapeutic landscape for estrogen-sensitive conditions ( ). Indeed, tamoxifen not only treats metastatic breast cancer but also serves as a chemo-preventive agent for high-risk women ( ). Following tamoxifen, subsequent generations like raloxifene and bazedoxifene expanded indications to include osteoporosis prevention and mitigation of menopausal vasomotor symptoms ( ; ), illustrating ongoing pharmaceutical innovation to refine efficacy and safety. Tamoxifen initial identification as an antifertility agent in animal models preceded its clinical approval in 1977 for metastatic breast cancer ( ). In 1998, it gained further FDA approval as a chemo-preventive drug demonstrating efficacy in lowering breast cancer risk among high-risk populations ( ; ). Similarly, raloxifene underwent rigorous clinical evaluation with FDA approval in 1998 for osteoporosis prevention and treatment, followed by approval in 2007 for breast cancer risk reduction ( ). Bazedoxifene, a third-generation SERM, received FDA approval in 2013 for treating vasomotor symptoms and preventing postmenopausal osteoporosis ( ). Moreover, numerous novel SERMs with unique pharmacological profiles have been developed over recent decades to address diverse therapeutic needs, extending the clinical armamentarium against estrogen-responsive diseases. The advent of SERMs marked a turning point in gynecologic oncology and bone health management. Tamoxifen and raloxifene continue as pivotal treatments for ER-positive breast cancer and osteoporosis prevention, with robust evidence supporting their efficacy in maintaining favorable lipid profiles and reducing breast cancer incidence among high-risk women ( ; ). Clinical trials further substantiate that raloxifene and bazedoxifene significantly reduce vertebral fractures in postmenopausal women, reinforcing their role in bone health ( ). Beyond bone and cancer protection, SERMs have been investigated for contraception, ovulatory dysfunction, and even improvements in skin aging ( ; ). Overall, these benefits underscore the broad impact of SERMs on gynecologic health and highlight their potential for wider therapeutic use. Continued research into optimizing tissue selectivity and minimizing adverse effects is crucial to fully realize their clinical potential. The molecular basis of SERMs’ tissue selectivity lies in their differential affinity for ERα and ERβ ( ). Overall, these benefits underscore the broad impact of SERMs on gynecologic health and highlight their potential for wider therapeutic use. Continued research into optimizing tissue selectivity and minimizing adverse effects is crucial to fully realize their clinical potential. The molecular basis of SERMs’ tissue selectivity lies in their differential affinity for ERα and ERβ ( ). This binding initiates complex intracellular signaling involving recruitment of coactivators and corepressors that ultimately dictate transcriptional, and consequently cellular, responses ( ) ( ). Typically, SERMs antagonize ERβ -mediated gene expression at EREs while exhibiting partial agonist activity via ERα ( ). The presence of GPER1 in ERα-positive breast cancer cells has been shown to alter tamoxifen sensitivity, although the mechanism remains unclear ( ). This illustrates the complex receptor dynamics underpinning SERM actions. These ligand-receptor interactions and conformational changes govern the distinct agonistic or antagonistic effects observed across tissues, forming the cornerstone of SERM pharmacology. Despite their unquestioned therapeutic value, the use of SERMs is not without adverse effects, which may indeed limit their clinical use. Common complications include thromboembolic events, osteoporosis, and even carcinogenesis. Findings from the NSABP P-1 trial highlight tamoxifen’s association with increased risks of endometrial cancer, vasomotor symptoms, cataracts, stroke, pulmonary embolism (PE), and drug resistance development ( ; ; ). Conversely, raloxifene displays a more favorable safety profile, lacking increased endometrial cancer risk and reducing breast cancer incidence, as confirmed in the MORE trial ( ). The ideal SERM exhibits antagonism in breast and uterine tissues coupled with agonism in bone and cardiovascular systems, maximizing benefit while mitigating risks ( ). Clinical decision-making must therefore be individualized, carefully balancing therapeutic efficacy and safety to optimize patient outcomes. 3.2 Pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of tamoxifen and raloxifene Pharmacokinetically, tamoxifen ( ) is a lipophilic prodrug extensively metabolized in the liver, predominantly by the cytochrome P450 enzyme CYP2D6, into active metabolites such as 4-hydroxytamoxifen, which exhibits 30 to 100-fold greater potency than the parent molecule ( ). This metabolic activation is crucial for tamoxifen’s clinical efficacy, yet CYP2D6 polymorphisms generate significant inter-individual variability in drug response, especially in ER-positive breast cancer patients ( ). Additional biotransformation by CYP3A4 and other enzymes produce metabolites that circulate systemically and engage target tissues before excretion mainly via feces ( ). Thus, tamoxifen’s therapeutic response and toxicity are influenced by the patient’s metabolic phenotype. Mechanistically, tamoxifen induces cancer cell death through multifactorial pathways. It activates caspase-9, inhibits epidermal growth factor receptor signaling, and disrupts mitochondrial function by impeding respiratory complexes I and III and modulating mitochondrial permeability transition pores, promoting apoptosis ( ; ). Tamoxifen also regulates gene expression involved in epithelial-mesenchymal transition, downregulating oncogenic regulators such as PLK1 , BIRC5 , and RACGAP1 , while upregulating tumor suppressor genes including MYLK , SOCS3 , and STAT5B , impacting breast cancer metastasis ( ). Long-term tamoxifen usage perturbs hepatic estrogen homeostasis by downregulating UGT2B gene expression, which may contribute to adverse effects like hepatotoxicity ( ). Cumulatively, tamoxifen initiates mitophagy, necrosis, apoptosis, and autophagy in ER-positive cancer cells via diverse signaling mechanisms. Raloxifene’s pharmacokinetics contrast markedly with tamoxifen; it exhibits low oral bioavailability (∼2%) due to extensive first-pass metabolism predominantly via glucuronidation by UGT1A2 ( ; ; ). Alternative delivery routes, such as transdermal, buccal, rectal, and nanoparticle-mediated systems like solid lipid nanoparticles, have shown promise in enhancing systemic exposure ( ). The major raloxifene metabolites, raloxifene-4′-glucuronide and raloxifene-6-glucuronide, are chiefly eliminated via feces with negligible renal clearance ( ). Raloxifene’s bioavailability and clearance are additionally modulated by factors including age, administration route, and ethnicity. Raloxifene’s tissue selectivity is primarily driven by structural elements, where the 6-hydroxy substituents confer estrogenic agonist activity and the piperidine side chain mediates antiestrogenic antagonism ( ). This antagonistic action is achieved through the ligand-receptor interaction that prevents coactivator binding in certain tissues, such as the breast and uterus ( ). Beyond direct ER modulation, raloxifene beneficially influences cardiovascular and metabolic pathways: it enhances endothelial function by increasing the NO to endothelin-1 ratio, reduces plasma homocysteine—an independent cardiovascular risk factor—and inhibits α-glucosidase, suggesting potential in glycemic control ( ). Furthermore, raloxifene disrupts cholesterol biosynthesis pathways leading to autophagy induction, which may contribute both to its chemotherapeutic effects and metabolic regulatory properties ( ). These combined actions render raloxifene effective not only for bone and breast protection but also for cardiovascular and metabolic health support. Despite their clinical efficacy, both tamoxifen and raloxifene face challenges due to acquired drug resistance. This has galvanized research into novel SERMs with enhanced tissue selectivity and safety profiles ( ). These combined actions render raloxifene effective not only for bone and breast protection but also for cardiovascular and metabolic health support. Despite their clinical efficacy, both tamoxifen and raloxifene face challenges due to acquired drug resistance. This has galvanized research into novel SERMs with enhanced tissue selectivity and safety profiles ( ). Bazedoxifene, a third-generation SERM, demonstrates efficacy in antiestrogen-resistant breast cancer models, progressing both preclinically and clinically ( ). Moreover, investigational compounds, including naphthalene, anthracenes, benzopyrans, indolones, genistein, indoles, and tetrahydroisoquinolines, are currently undergoing evaluation ( ). Interestingly, the development of selective estrogen receptor down-regulators also offers emerging alternative or complementary therapeutic options for SERM-resistant malignancies ( ). Despite such developments, tamoxifen and raloxifene remain the most utilized SERMs in clinical practice. The functional diversity of SERMs is rooted in the dynamic interplay between ligand binding and ER conformational states, which dictate coactivator or corepressor recruitment and subsequent transcriptional activation or repression ( ; ; ; ) ( ). Tamoxifen and raloxifene predominantly adopt receptor configurations that favor corepressor interaction, thereby inhibiting the formation of the transcription initiation complexes necessary for estrogen response element binding and gene transcription activation ( ). While the complex landscape of ER modulation remains incompletely understood, ongoing studies continue to unravel the multilayered regulatory mechanisms involving various co-regulators that ultimately determine the tissue-specific and context-dependent effects of SERMs. Collectively, these pharmacokinetic and mitochondrial-disruptive properties of tamoxifen provide a mechanistic framework through which off-target oxidative stress and altered redox signaling may extend beyond tumor cells to the vasculature, potentially contributing to endothelial dysfunction and increased thrombotic susceptibility observed in susceptible patient populations. 3.3 Molecular mechanisms of SERMs effects on cardiovascular physiology SERMs influence cardiovascular physiology predominantly through their tissue-specific interactions with ERα and ERβ expressed in endothelial and smooth muscle cells. ERα, highly abundant in endothelial cells, is essential for vascular protection, primarily by mitigating angiotensin II–induced hypertension via its transcriptional activity at the AF2 domain ( ; ). This role is evidenced by worsened hypertensive phenotypes in ERα knockout female mice. Pharmacologic activation with selective ERα agonists such as Cpd1471 restores endothelial nitric oxide synthase (eNOS) expression and endothelial function, underscoring ERα′s pivotal contribution to vascular homeostasis ( ). In parallel, ERβ attenuates vasoconstriction, reduces vascular resistance, and lowers blood pressure; genetic loss of ERβ disrupts vascular contractility and ion channel function, exacerbating hypertension ( ). Administration of selective ERβ agonists like 8β-VE2 effectively lowers systolic blood pressure and vascular resistance ( ). This highlights the complementary and synergistic roles of ERα and ERβ in maintaining vascular function and positioning SERMs as promising agents in hypertensive management. Beyond classical genomic signaling, SERMs engage in rapid non-genomic pathways ( ). Raloxifene, for example, stimulates NO production via ERα-PI3K interaction, enhancing vascular reactivity and promoting vasodilation ( ). ERβ activation mitigates vascular inflammation and atherosclerotic progression, while ERα facilitates myocardial glucose uptake ( ). In hypertensive models, ERβ upregulation correlates with increased hypoxia-inducible factor-1α (HIF-1α) activity, promoting adaptive vascular remodeling and cardiopulmonary protection ( ). Collectively, these mechanisms extend SERM benefits beyond cancer prevention to comprehensive cardiometabolic health support. While raloxifene and tamoxifen both increase venous thromboembolism (VTE) risk similarly to estrogen, their long-term cardiovascular impact remains incompletely characterized. Both agents induce acute coronary artery relaxation mediated by NO release, promoting vasodilation ( ); however, their effectiveness in reducing atherosclerotic plaque burden is limited, as demonstrated in hypercholesterolemic models ( ). Large-scale clinical trials such as STAR and RUTH continue to investigate cardiovascular outcomes associated with SERMs, yet detailed understanding of their effects on venous vasculature, endothelial signaling, and vascular smooth muscle cell function remains insufficient ( ; ). Notably, the STAR trial revealed that raloxifene reduces thromboembolic events by approximately 30% compared to tamoxifen, particularly lowering risks of PE and deep vein thrombosis ( ). Despite this, both SERMs favorably influence cardiovascular risk markers, including lipid profiles, homocysteine, and C-reactive protein levels, potentially contributing to their vascular protective effects ( ). The interplay between these benefits and thrombotic risks highlights the complexity of SERM cardiovascular pharmacology and necessitates careful, individualized clinical monitoring. The balance between efficacy and safety is delicate and demands further elucidation through ongoing research. SERMs robustly enhance endothelial function by stimulating eNOS activation, leading to an increased NO bioavailability and improved vascular tone ( ). The activation of eNOS occurs through multiple mechanisms, including phosphorylation mediated by kinases such as Akt via ERα-PI3K interactions, as well as calcium/calmodulin binding, both of which promote robust NO production critical for vasodilation ( ). ERβ further contributes by suppressing vascular inflammation and slowing atherosclerosis progression, while ERα maintains eNOS expression to preserve endothelial resilience, particularly under hypertensive conditions.

SERMs robustly enhance endothelial function by stimulating eNOS activation, leading to an increased NO bioavailability and improved vascular tone ( ). The activation of eNOS occurs through multiple mechanisms, including phosphorylation mediated by kinases such as Akt via ERα-PI3K interactions, as well as calcium/calmodulin binding, both of which promote robust NO production critical for vasodilation ( ). ERβ further contributes by suppressing vascular inflammation and slowing atherosclerosis progression, while ERα maintains eNOS expression to preserve endothelial resilience, particularly under hypertensive conditions. Additionally, the G-protein-coupled receptor GPR30 augments pulmonary NO synthesis, alleviating right ventricular overload and reducing myocardial fibrosis ( ). Together, ERα and ERβ synergistically regulate pulmonary vascular tone, underscoring eNOS activation as a central mechanism through which SERMs confer vascular protection ( ). This robust endothelial modulation by SERMs is foundational to their cardiovascular benefits. SERMs, including tamoxifen and raloxifene, intricately affect the coagulation system and platelet function, producing a complex balance between potential antithrombotic and prothrombotic effects ( ). Both agents consistently reduce plasma fibrinogen, a key coagulation glycoprotein, which may lower thrombotic risk ( ). However, the effects of SERMs on other coagulation factors such as factor VII, antithrombin III, and plasminogen activator inhibitor-1 (PAI-1) remain inconsistent across studies, leaving their overall influence on thrombotic risk unclear. Importantly, despite potential anticoagulant effects, clinical evidence robustly associates SERMs with elevated VTE risk, mirroring the known thrombotic profile of estrogen therapy ( ). Albeit through distinct mechanisms, both tamoxifen and raloxifene modulate platelet aggregation, a critical step in thrombogenesis. Tamoxifen enhances platelet activation by promoting ROS generation via an NADPH oxidase-dependent pathway, with its active metabolite 4-hydroxy-tamoxifen further amplifying this effect by increasing platelet superoxide release, thereby intensifying pro-thrombotic potential ( ). Interestingly, tamoxifen’s influence on platelets is context-dependent, exhibiting both pro- and anti-aggregatory properties depending on the vascular and cellular environment. Raloxifene, in contrast, may exert more favorable vascular effects by not only enhancing NO production, a known inhibitor of platelet aggregation ( ) but also by directly inhibiting aggregation. This dual action contributes to raloxifene’s overall vascular protective profile ( ). Thus, while both SERMs affect platelet function, raloxifene’s enhancement of NO bioavailability likely confers a more favorable balance between platelet activation and inhibition compared to tamoxifen, highlighting the complex interplay between thrombotic risk and vascular protection inherent in SERM therapy. In hormone-sensitive breast cancer, platelet activation is further intensified through direct platelet-tumor cell interactions, wherein tamoxifen upregulates platelet adhesion molecules like P-selectin on certain breast cancer cells ( ). This promotes platelet aggregation and fibrin network formation, contributing to a hypercoagulable state and increased thrombosis risk in patients receiving SERM therapy ( ). Altogether, these diverse, context-specific actions of SERMs on coagulation cascades and platelet physiology underline the critical need for individualized risk assessment and vigilant clinical monitoring to balance therapeutic benefits against thrombotic hazards. From a translational standpoint, the balance between ERα-, ERβ-, and GPR30-mediated signaling emerges as a critical determinant of vascular outcome. While SERMs can enhance nitric oxide bioavailability and attenuate vascular inflammation, concurrent activation of redox-sensitive platelet and coagulation pathways may offset these benefits, offering a mechanistic explanation for the discordance between favorable vascular biomarkers and persistent thromboembolic risk in clinical settings. 4 Vascular benefits of SERMs SERMS exert multifaceted effects on cardiovascular health, extending well beyond their established role in modulating thrombotic risk. Their actions include enhancements of endothelial function, regulation of lipid metabolism, and engagement of broader cardioprotective pathways that may collective influence vascular integrity and disease outcomes ( ). By promoting NO bioavailability, stabilizing cholesterol levels, and potentially improving systemic metabolic parameters, SERMs emerge as agents capable of reducing atherosclerotic burden and mitigating the risk of coronary artery disease ( ). These mechanisms position SERMs at the interface between endocrine modulation and cardiovascular protection, warranting detailed examination of their vascular effects ( ) ( ). 4.1 Endothelial function and oxidative stress One of the most consistent cardiovascular effects of SERMs is the preservation of endothelial homeostasis. Endothelial cells represent the first line of defense against vascular injury, and their dysfunction is a pivotal step in atherogenesis. SERMs, particularly raloxifene, enhance NO production through rapid activation of endothelial eNOS, thereby improving vasodilation and vascular remodeling ( ). NO confers widespread vascular protection by reducing vascular resistance, suppressing platelet aggregation, and attenuating the expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines and adhesion molecules ( ). In parallel, SERMs influence VSMC proliferation, apoptosis, and intracellular calcium dynamics, processes central to vascular remodeling and the maintenance of arterial elasticity. These protective effects converge with endogenous estrogen pathways, whereby estrogen reduce adhesion molecule expression and stimulate vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) synthesis, thereby facilitating angiogenesis and re-reendothelialization after injury ( ). At a complementary level of intracellular regulation,
