This assessment includes the evaluation of technical candidacy and potential procedural risk of each option, a heart team discussion, and consideration of patient preferences, cognitive function, and life expectancy. A heart team discussion regarding treatment of an older patient would include treatment options including guideline-directed medical therapy, PCI, and CABG. Coronary anatomy, comorbidities, procedural factors, and patient factors should be considered. It is also recommended that patient preferences, cognitive function, and life expectancy be considered when determining revascularization strategy in older patients. Shared decision-making including the patient and the patient’s support system allows for consideration of the financial impact of treatment on the patient and the patient’s family, the impact of alteration of QoL after treatment, the patient’s personal goals and cultural beliefs, the patient’s health literacy, and social determinants of health. An older patient who is employed may decide on the least invasive option to facilitate return to work, or may prefer to prioritize QoL and a short hospitalization over longer-term benefits. Important patient factors to consider in revascularization treatment decisions include comorbidities, frailty, nutritional status, immunocompetence, functional and cognitive status, availability of social support, likelihood and safety of dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) adherence, need for other cardiac procedures, and estimated life expectancy. , Technical feasibility and procedural risk are also considered when evaluating revascularization treatment options in older patients. Important considerations for CABG include calculation of the Society of Thoracic Surgeons Predicted Risk of Mortality; the size and degree of calcification of the coronary arteries and likely potential for grafting; the available conduit for bypasses, including the left internal mammary artery; the degree of calcification of the ascending aorta (to permit cannulation, cross clamp, and placement of proximal anastomoses); and left ventricular ejection fraction. Calculation of the Society of Thoracic Surgeons Predicted Risk of Mortality is recommended when considering CABG ; however, in a 75-year-old patient with 3-vessel CAD, the Society of Thoracic Surgeons Predicted Risk of Mortality is only 0.034% higher than that of a 74-year-old patient, which increases by only 0.328% in an 80-year-old patient. When considering the technical feasibility of PCI, assessment of possible access site complications, degree of coronary calcification, presence of trifurcation lesions (particularly with left main stenosis), tortuosity of target vessel, length of lesion to be treated, the potential success of crossing a coronary lesion, and the potential need for hemodynamic support is important. After consideration of both coronary revascularization options, it may be evident that one option is more appropriate than another in the older patient ( ). CABG is often more appropriate in patients with multivessel CAD, complex left main stenosis, diabetes, low left ventricular ejection fraction with suitable anatomy, contraindication to DAPT therapy, or severe in-stent restenosis. PCI is often more appropriate in patients with advanced age, reduced life expectancy, or severe left ventricular dysfunction combined with high surgical risk factors, including frailty, poor functional or cognitive status, multiple comorbidities, severely calcified or porcelain aorta, poor bypass conduit, or lack of bypass conduit. In those high-risk older patients, PCI can achieve meaningful symptom relief with lower up-front morbidity risk. These are consistent with findings in patients with 3-vessel or left main disease who underwent PCI after they were determined to be ineligible for CABG after a heart team discussion. The most common reasons for CABG ineligibility were poor conduits, severe systolic dysfunction, advanced age, severe cerebrovascular disease, severe lung disease, renal insufficiency, malignancy, severe peripheral artery disease, morbid obesity, or cachexia ( ). COMPLETE VERSUS CULPRIT-ONLY REVASCULARIZATION IN OLDER ADULTS Several trials have investigated the question of culprit-only versus complete revascularization in patients with ACS, but most have excluded older patients (≥75 years of age). The COMPLETE trial (Complete vs Culprit-Only Revascularization to Treat Multivessel Disease After Early PCI for STEMI) demonstrated that complete revascularization was superior to culprit-only revascularization at reducing death or MI in patients presenting with STEMI. The mean age of the 4041 participants enrolled in this trial was 62 years. The FULL REVASC trial (FFR-Guidance for Complete Non-Culprit Revascularization) evaluated physiology-guided complete revascularization compared with usual care among 1542 patients with STEMI and multivessel CAD who underwent culprit vessel PCI. The mean age of participants enrolled in that trial was 65 years. There is sparse evidence regarding the benefits and risks of complete versus culprit-only revascularization in older adults (≥75 years) presenting with ACS. The FULL REVASC trial (FFR-Guidance for Complete Non-Culprit Revascularization) evaluated physiology-guided complete revascularization compared with usual care among 1542 patients with STEMI and multivessel CAD who underwent culprit vessel PCI. The mean age of participants enrolled in that trial was 65 years. There is sparse evidence regarding the benefits and risks of complete versus culprit-only revascularization in older adults (≥75 years) presenting with ACS. The FIRE trial (Functional Assessment in Elderly MI Patients With Multivessel Disease)—which enrolled 1445 participants age ≥75 years from 34 sites in Italy, Spain, or Poland who were admitted with STEMI or NSTEMI, underwent successful PCI of the culprit lesion, and had multivessel disease with ≥1 nonculprit lesion with a minimum vessel diameter of 2.5 mm and a visually estimated stenosis of 50% to 99%—attempted to bridge this evidence gap. After successful culprit PCI, patients were randomized to receive either culprit-only treatment or physiology-guided complete revascularization. Patients in the physiology-guided complete revascularization group underwent PCI of all functionally significant nonculprit lesions. Patients in the culprit-only group did not receive additional physiologic assessment or nonculprit lesion revascularization. The primary outcome was a composite of death, MI, stroke, or ischemia-driven coronary revascularization occurring at 1 year. The primary outcome occurred in 113 patients (15.7%) in the complete revascularization group and 152 patients (21.0%) in the culprit-only group, with a number needed to treat (benefit) of 19 patients. Secondary outcomes included a composite end point of cardiovascular death or MI at 1 year, which was also reduced with a physiology-guided complete revascularization strategy compared with a culprit-only strategy. All individual components of the primary outcome except for stroke were lower in the physiology-guided complete revascularization group. There was no difference between the 2 groups in terms of the incidence of a composite of contrast-associated acute kidney injury, stroke, or bleeding at 1 year. Data from this trial provided insights into the safety and efficacy of physiology-guided complete revascularization in older patients with ACS and multivessel disease. A meta-analysis of trials evaluating complete versus culprit-only revascularization that included older adults, including the FIRE results and the COMPLETE subgroup analysis results of participants ≥75 years of age, found that complete revascularization was associated with reduced MACEs without significant concomitant increases in acute renal injury or major bleeding. COMPLETE-2—a prospective, multicenter RCT comparing a strategy of physiology-guided complete revascularization with angiography-guided complete revascularization in patients with STEMI or NSTEMI and multivessel CAD who have undergone successful culpritlesion PCI—is underway. COMPLETE-2 is planning to enroll all adults with no age cutoff; inclusion of older adults will supplement the current evidence provided by the FIRE trial on complete revascularization in older adults. AORTIC STENOSIS AND CAD IN OLDER ADULT POPULATIONS Aortic stenosis is a disease of the aging population that is frequently observed with concomitant CAD. The widespread adoption of TAVR has offered a less-invasive treatment option for patients diagnosed with severe aortic stenosis. This has been particularly beneficial for older adults, many of whom were previously deemed at high risk or inoperable for surgical aortic valve replacement. Data from PARTNER I (Placement of Aortic Transcatheter Valve Trial), which only included the highest-risk patients, showed that there was significant mortality benefit associated with TAVR compared with medical management, even in this high-risk population. There is often considerable overlap between symptoms of CAD and aortic stenosis, as well as a large proportion of patients (15%–80%) who are found to have both disease processes. The 2020 American College of Cardiology/AHA guideline for the management of patients with valvular heart disease recommends an individualized approach to treatment of CAD before TAVR, and that patients with substantial left main or proximal CAD undergo revascularization before TAVR. The NOTION-3 trial (Revascularization in Patients Undergoing Transcatheter Aortic Valve Implantation) investigated the impact of performing PCI alongside TAVR in patients with both severe aortic stenosis and CAD. The study found that patients who underwent PCI had a significantly lower incidence of MACEs—defined as death, MI, or urgent revascularization—compared with those receiving only conservative treatment. However, PCI was also associated with an increased risk of bleeding. These findings suggest that PCI may offer benefits for certain patients undergoing TAVR, but risks such as bleeding complications must be considered. For others, it is recommended and safe to proceed with valve replacement and then reassess symptoms to help guide management. This is likely even more relevant among the older adult population of patients, where revascularization and postprocedure DAPT carry additional risk and management considerations. The timing of intervention is an important consideration. Revascularization before, simultaneous with, or after TAVR are potential options. The risks and benefits of staged versus combined procedures must be weighed. In appropriately selected older adults with concurrent aortic stenosis and CAD, treatment strategies may include TAVR with staged or concomitant PCI or surgical aortic valve replacement with CABG. The choice should be guided by anatomic complexity, frailty, surgical risk, and patient-centered goals of care. Chronic kidney disease is more common in the older adult population, and in this scenario, it may be prudent to stage the PCI and TAVR procedures rather than combining them. For patients with high-risk coronary anatomy or where there may be difficulty accessing the coronaries after TAVR valve implantation, revascularization before TAVR is likely beneficial. For an individual with critical aortic stenosis, the TAVR procedure likely takes priority. Beyond timing, there may be less concern regarding the need to reaccess the coronary arteries after TAVR in older compared with younger patients, which can influence the decision regarding type of TAVR valve. Overall, revascularization surrounding the timing of TAVR should be individualized in terms of whether to revascularize as well as timing of revascularization while weighing the unique patient-specific clinical and anatomic risks versus benefits of coronary revascularization. APPROACH FOR OLDER ADULTS AND TECHNICAL CONSIDERATIONS Advancements in health care delivery systems, critical care management, technical expertise, and device technology have allowed the application of PCI and other endovascular procedures to older and higher-risk patients. With respect to older patients with ACS and complex CAD requiring PCI, for example, advancements have resulted in significant improvements in survival and QoL. However, older patients are at elevated risk of procedural morbidity and mortality, and age and geriatric syndromes affect both short- and long-term outcomes of procedural interventions. The optimization of procedural outcomes in older adults requires comprehensive patient assessment; appropriate patient selection; awareness of age-specific physiologic, anatomic, and clinical challenges; and strict adherence to general and age-specific procedural best practices. Fundamental to patient selection is understanding the relative benefits versus risks associated with a given procedure. Various online resources and mobile apps can assist in this endeavor, including the Society of Thoracic Surgeons/American College of Cardiology TAVR In-Hospital Mortality Risk tool, the TIMI and GRACE risk scores for assessment of in-hospital and 6-month mortality risk in STEMI, and the Society for Cardiovascular Angiography & Interventions PCI Risk tool for predicting peri-PCI morbidity and mortality. Beyond risk prevention models, clinical experience and implementation of heart team models, inclusive of geriatrics and palliative care medicine, are imperative in complex medical decision-making involving elderly patients and identification of when interventions should be considered futile. Understanding and respecting patient values and preferences is necessary when weighing the potential tradeoffs of complex cardiovascular interventions and crucial to the shared decision-making process. Despite proven benefits of the shared decision-making process, its application in older adults can be complicated by cognitive and sensory impairments, caregiver dependence, involvement of multiple family members and their respective viewpoints and opinions, acuity of presentation, and limitations on clinician time and ability to effectively communicate the necessary information. , Various age-related factors can complicate procedural-related success and safety. The process of cardiovascular and renal aging contributes to endothelial dysfunction, increased systemic inflammation, increased arterial stiffness and calcification, decreased responsiveness to beta-adrenergic stimulation, impaired ventricular relaxation, and renal tubular dysfunction with altered sodium and potassium handling and urine-concentrating ability. These changes can in turn greatly affect the older patient’s ability to tolerate changes in hemodynamics incurred with sedation, blood loss, or acute cardiac conditions. These conditions demand increased attention to preprocedural planning and intraprocedural attention to hemodynamics and respiratory status, adherence to best practices in endovascular techniques and protocols, and knowledge of age-related sensitivities to medications and required dose adjustments. , , PHARMACOTHERAPY IN PATIENTS UNDERGOING CORONARY REVASCULARIZATION Age-related pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic changes are important considerations in selecting procedural pharmacotherapy in older patients undergoing revascularization. Reduced renal and hepatic function can lead to prolonged duration of administered medications, changes in body composition can affect drug distribution, and altered receptor sensitivity can affect response to medications in older patients undergoing PCI ( ). Conscious sedation is frequently administered during PCI, with the most commonly used regimen consisting of a benzodiazepine and an opiate antagonist. Limited data exist evaluating the best approach to moderate sedation in older patients undergoing cardiac catheterization; therefore, society guidance considerations have been proposed. , For older patients, proposed considerations include to use an opioid-based regimen without benzodiazepines in an effort to avoid delirium while keeping in mind the potential delay in antiplatelet onset in oral P2Y12-naive patients. Additional considerations include using lower initial doses of sedating and pain medication to balance comfort and safety. DAPT with aspirin plus an oral P2Y12 inhibitor is the mainstay of therapy to prevent thrombotic events in older patients undergoing PCI. When selecting an oral P2Y12, consideration should be given to the agent selected, clinical presentation, timing of angiography, concomitant medications, and the risk for thrombotic and adverse events. For patients with SIHD undergoing PCI, guidelines provide a Class 1 recommendation for clopidogrel in addition to aspirin to reduce ischemic events, regardless of age. In addition, in the absence of known coronary anatomy, the guidelines state that evidence does not support routine pretreatment before angiography. For older people presenting with ACS who undergo PCI, some variability has been observed with trial results of oral P2Y12 therapy over time. A substudy of the PLATO trial (A Comparison of Ticagrelor [AZD6140] and Clopidogrel in Patients With Acute Coronary Syndrome) that assessed outcomes of ticagrelor versus clopidogrel in patients ≥75 years of age compared with those <75 years of age reported that the clinical benefit and overall safety of ticagrelor versus clopidogrel was not significantly different in older versus younger patients. Approximately 73% of patients ≥75 years of age underwent PCI during the conduct of the trial. More recently, the POPular AGE trial (Ticagrelor or Prasugrel Versus Clopidogrel in Elderly Patients With an Acute Coronary Syndrome and a High Bleeding Risk: Optimization of Antiplatelet Treatment in High-Risk Elderly) randomized patients ≥70 years of age with NSTE-ACS to clopidogrel versus ticagrelor or prasugrel, and results showed significantly fewer bleeding events in the clopidogrel group without an increase in the composite ischemic end point. In this trial, ≈50% of patients underwent PCI, and no interaction was observed. Guidelines suggest cautious use of prasugrel in patients ≥75 years of age on the basis of the results of the TRITON trial (A Comparison of Prasugrel [CS-747] and Clopidogrel in Acute Coronary Syndrome Subjects Who Are to Undergo Percutaneous Coronary Intervention), which used a 10-mg maintenance dose of prasugrel and showed no net clinical benefit of prasugrel versus clopidogrel in patients ≥75 years of age due to higher rates of bleeding. Recent trials have assessed a 5-mg maintenance dose of prasugrel in older people undergoing PCI. The Elderly ACS 2 trial randomized patients with ACS >74 years of age and undergoing PCI to clopidogrel or a reduced dose of prasugrel (5 mg daily). The trial was stopped early due to futility, but no significant differences in the primary composite ischemic end point were observed, whereas the reported rate of major bleeding was numerically higher in the prasugrel group. In patients with atrial fibrillation undergoing PCI, minimizing bleeding risk while preserving anti-ischemic effects is crucial. Dual therapy with a direct oral anticoagulant plus clopidogrel is generally preferred over triple therapy, particularly in older adults, based on data from trials such as PIONEER AF-PCI (A Study Exploring Two Strategies of Rivaroxaban [JNJ39039039; BAY-59–7939] and One of Oral Vitamin K Antagonist in Patients With Atrial Fibrillation Who Undergo Percutaneous Coronary Intervention) and AUGUSTUS (A Study of Apixaban in Patients With Atrial Fibrillation, Not Caused by a

observed, whereas the reported rate of major bleeding was numerically higher in the prasugrel group. In patients with atrial fibrillation undergoing PCI, minimizing bleeding risk while preserving anti-ischemic effects is crucial. Dual therapy with a direct oral anticoagulant plus clopidogrel is generally preferred over triple therapy, particularly in older adults, based on data from trials such as PIONEER AF-PCI (A Study Exploring Two Strategies of Rivaroxaban [JNJ39039039; BAY-59–7939] and One of Oral Vitamin K Antagonist in Patients With Atrial Fibrillation Who Undergo Percutaneous Coronary Intervention) and AUGUSTUS (A Study of Apixaban in Patients With Atrial Fibrillation, Not Caused by a Heart Valve Problem, Who Are at Risk for Thrombosis [Blood Clots] Due to Having Had a Recent Coronary Event, Such as a Heart Attack or a Procedure to Open the Vessels of the Heart). , These regimens reduce bleeding events without a significant increase in thrombotic complications. Guidelines do not recommend the routine use of intravenous platelet inhibitors during PCI. Glycoprotein IIb/IIIa antagonists receive a 2a recommendation for use in patients with ACS undergoing PCI with a large thrombus burden or no or slow reflow; cangrelor receives a 2b recommendation as a reasonable strategy to reduce periprocedural ischemia during PCI in oral P2Y12-naive patients. A subanalysis of CHAMPION PHOENIX (A Clinical Trial Comparing Cangrelor to Clopidogrel Standard Therapy in Subjects Who Require Percutaneous Coronary Intervention) reported no increase in major bleeding and similar efficacy of cangrelor compared with clopidogrel in patients ≥75 years of age compared with those <75 years of age. Given the concern about bleeding risk with longer-term DAPT in older patients who have undergone PCI, recent strategies such as shortening the course of DAPT and antiplatelet deescalation (either early discontinuation of aspirin or changing from ticagrelor or prasugrel to clopidogrel after 1 to 3 months with or without the guidance of genotyping of platelet function testing) have been studied in an attempt to balance bleeding and ischemic risk. A recently published systematic review of different durations of DAPT in older adults after PCI reported that abbreviated DAPT durations were associated with lower rates of bleeding with no observed increase in MACE rates. Studies of deescalation strategies have shown reduced bleeding with no apparent increase in ischemic events, but most of the research has been conducted in patients of East Asian descent. Unfractionated heparin (UFH) is the anticoagulant used most often during PCI in the United States. Guidelines provide a Class 1 recommendation for UFH during PCI to reduce ischemic events. A Class 2b recommendation is made for bivalirudin as a reasonable alternative to UFH to reduce bleeding; intravenous enoxaparin at the time of PCI receives a 2b recommendation in patients with NSTE-ACS started on subcutaneous enoxaparin before PCI. A subanalysis of patients ≥75 years of age enrolled in the VALIDATE-SWEEDEHEART trial (Bivalirudin versus Heparin in ST-Segment and Non-ST-Segment Elevation Myocardial Infarction in Patients on Modern Antiplatelet Therapy in the Swedish Web System for Enhancement and Development of Evidence-Based Care in Heart Disease Evaluated According to Recommended Therapies Registry Trial) reported no differences in ischemic or bleeding outcomes between the UFH and bivalirudin groups, suggesting that bivalirudin may be a safe alternative to UFH in older patients undergoing PCI. As discussed, age-related changes that can affect the pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of medications as well as the potential for drug–drug interactions due to polypharmacy are important considerations when prescribing medications in older patients undergoing CABG. In general, a heart team discussion should be considered when making perioperative medication choices for older patients undergoing CABG. Recent guidelines provide limited guidance on age-specific recommendations for medications in older patients undergoing CABG. However, given the observation of geriatric syndromes being associated with an increased risk for adverse procedural outcomes, it is important to review several of the recommendations. In patients undergoing CABG, the guidelines provide a Class 1 recommendation for the use of an intraoperative insulin infusion to maintain a serum glucose level <180 mg/dL to reduce the risk of a sternal would infection and a Class 1 recommendation for the continuation of aspirin until the time of surgery in patients already taking aspirin preoperatively. Because older people are at higher risk of CABG-associated bleeding complications, relevant recommendations include a Class 2a recommendation for patients undergoing elective CABG on an oral P2Y12 inhibitor to discontinue ticagrelor for 3 days, clopidogrel for 5 days, and prasugrel for 7 days before CABG to reduce the risk of major bleeding. A Class 3 recommendation is made for initiating aspirin in the immediate preoperative period in patients who were previously not on aspirin undergoing elective CABG. A recent systematic review reported age as being an independent risk factor for delirium after CABG. Given this, consideration should be given to anesthesia strategies and postoperative pain regimens that can reduce delirium risk. NONINTERVENTIONAL CONSIDERATIONS When considering treatment options

recommendation for patients undergoing elective CABG on an oral P2Y12 inhibitor to discontinue ticagrelor for 3 days, clopidogrel for 5 days, and prasugrel for 7 days before CABG to reduce the risk of major bleeding. A Class 3 recommendation is made for initiating aspirin in the immediate preoperative period in patients who were previously not on aspirin undergoing elective CABG. A recent systematic review reported age as being an independent risk factor for delirium after CABG. Given this, consideration should be given to anesthesia strategies and postoperative pain regimens that can reduce delirium risk. NONINTERVENTIONAL CONSIDERATIONS When considering treatment options for older adults presenting for potential revascularization, multidisciplinary team–based care, patient education, and shared decision-making are particularly important for a strategy that is patient-centered. Patient-centered care in geriatric cardiology integrates clinical expertise and the latest evidence with the patient’s health priorities, life goals, preferences, values, and beliefs. , Assessing what matters most to patients is foundational in shared decision-making. , Older adults are more likely than younger adults to prioritize the ability to remain independent, with a focus on maintaining mobility, functional status, and QoL rather than longevity. CR, a Class 1 recommendation for secondary prevention of adults undergoing coronary revascularization, provides an opportunity to deliver personalized approaches to cardiovascular and psychologic health in the context of their holistic health care needs. Care Coordination Continuity in care as older adults undergoing coronary revascularization transition from hospital to home or a rehabilitation facility is important given the greater prevalence of frailty, multimorbidity, depression, cognitive decline, diminished functional status, and higher symptom burden. Decisions may need to be made for appropriate levels of care (eg, intensive care, long-term care facility, hospice), advanced care (eg, surgical intervention), and multidisciplinary care coordination (eg, primary care physicians, advanced practitioners, palliative care, other specialists). To achieve optimum coordination of care, and in turn, optimal outcomes, a multidisciplinary team of physicians, geriatricians, nurses, exercise physiologists, dieticians, social workers, and the patient’s support network is essential. Geriatric comanagement is a model of care for older adults with medical complexity whereby a designated geriatrician or geriatrics-trained nurse provides concurrent care alongside the cardiovascular clinician. Shared Decision-Making Shared decision-making is a communication process by which patients and clinicians collaborate to choose treatments and care plans that most align with a patient’s preferences, beliefs, values, and health goals. Shared decision-making considering the patient’s preferences and goals of care is vital to personalized, holistic care of older adults. In shared decision-making, clinicians provide evidence-based information about reasonable options and the patient provides expertise on their personal situation, values, preferences, and attitude toward risk ( ). Because older adults—particularly older patients from underrepresented racial or ethnic groups and older women—have been underrepresented in cardiovascular clinical trials or excluded on the basis of age or comorbidities, the evidence base from clinical trials to facilitate shared decision-making is particularly sparse in terms of patient-centered outcomes such as symptoms, function, or QoL. Whereas older adults are a heterogeneous group, sharing medical information with older adults involves potential challenges, including cognitive impairment, hearing or visual impairment, and low health literacy. Contextual complexity, including multimorbidity, frailty, cognitive impairment, and social determinants of health, also presents challenges in shared decision-making. Situational complexity and social determinants of health may also influence disease burden, access to care, the choice of revascularization strategy, and health outcomes. Shared decision-making with older adults and their support network is enhanced with input from relevant multidisciplinary colleagues. In treatment decisions that have no single best choice, patient decision aids may be useful for older adults. The most recent Cochrane review of decision aids (209 studies involving 107 698 participants) found that decision aids resulted in improved knowledge, accurate risk perceptions, and an active role in decision-making. Advance Care Planning Helping patients and their families understand the risks and benefits of treatments for advanced CVD through advance care planning and advance directives is a common and important form of shared decision-making. The intent of palliative care is to improve QoL and reduce suffering among patients with serious illness. A 2016 AHA policy statement recognizes the benefits of advance care planning and shared decision-making in advanced CVD and suggests that “care planning and decision-making processes, including discussions concerning goals of care, postdischarge needs, options, and resources, are patient-directed and patient-centered and are conducted in consultation with the patient’s surrogate decision-makers, family caregivers, and professionals responsible for the patient’s care, including palliative care generalists and specialists as needed.” Patient Education The lack of synthesis of educational interventions for secondary prevention or structure of education delivery for older patients with CVD provides little guidance for practice. However, a meta-analysis of 73 studies (n=24 985; mean age, 60.5±5.7 years) found that patient education for secondary prevention, in various delivery modes and intensities, improved multiple self-reported health behaviors in patients with CAD.

goals of care, postdischarge needs, options, and resources, are patient-directed and patient-centered and are conducted in consultation with the patient’s surrogate decision-makers, family caregivers, and professionals responsible for the patient’s care, including palliative care generalists and specialists as needed.” Patient Education The lack of synthesis of educational interventions for secondary prevention or structure of education delivery for older patients with CVD provides little guidance for practice. However, a meta-analysis of 73 studies (n=24 985; mean age, 60.5±5.7 years) found that patient education for secondary prevention, in various delivery modes and intensities, improved multiple self-reported health behaviors in patients with CAD. Patient education also reduced anxiety and depressive symptoms in patients with coronary heart disease. Nurses are the most frequent providers of educational interventions, particularly at hospital discharge and outpatient care, to ensure follow-up at home. In many nurse-led CR programs, nurses work collaboratively with other health care professionals to deliver patient education on the management of CVD risk factors, nutrition counseling, psychosocial interventions, and tobacco cessation interventions. Cardiac Rehabilitation CR is a multidisciplinary, systematic yet personalized program to help patients achieve cardiovascular health and guideline-directed targets for control of risk factors. The AHA/American College of Cardiology provides a Class 1 recommendation for center-based CR for patients undergoing coronary revascularization. Evidence substantiates the role of center-based CR (CBCR) exercise participation for improving CVD risk factors and reducing recurrent CVD adverse events and mortality risk in older adults. Systematic reviews and meta-analyses of RCTs of CR have consistently demonstrated these outcome benefits in patients with ACS after coronary revascularization and heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, although the mean age of trial participants was 56 years (range, 44–77). CR provides an opportunity to develop personalized approaches to cardiovascular health in the context of older adults’ aggregate health care challenges. , In addition, CBCR fosters socialization among older adults who otherwise may have limited social options. Furthermore, CR provides a unique opportunity for both medication reconciliation and direct observation of tolerance of medications during supervised exercise, allowing for a patient-centered approach to optimize medical therapy while reducing risks of adverse events, particularly falls, in older adults. Despite the benefits of CR, participation declines with increasing patient age, and only 25% of older patients eligible for CR participate or complete the program. Women also tend to participate less often than men across all ages, but because women tend to outlive men, these gaps worsen among older adults. Common barriers to CBCR among older adults include a lack of understanding among patients and clinicians of the value of CBCR, prohibitive logistics given that many older adults cannot drive, unaffordable copayments for CBCR for patients on fixed incomes, and inflexibility in format to achieve personalized therapeutic approaches in CBCR that are tailored to the wide range of needs and circumstances among older adults. To address barriers to attendance and extend the reach of secondary prevention services, home-based CR or hybrid CR models of care have been developed. A scientific statement summarizing evidence on home-based CR with either synchronous or asynchronous communication reported short-term benefits that were similar to those with CBCR. Home-based CR consists of the core components of CBCR programs but is delivered through regular contact with health care professionals through telephone calls or mobile technology. Home-based CR is reasonable to consider for low- to moderate-risk patients who otherwise cannot attend traditional CBCR, although efficacy for adults with frailty or cognitive impairment, or who are prone to falls, is unclear. GAPS IN KNOWLEDGE AND FUTURE DIRECTIONS Gaps in knowledge regarding coronary revascularization in older adults persist due to limited representation in clinical trials. Evidence is needed to guide revascularization strategies, timing, and approach in the context of frailty, multimorbidity, and other geriatric syndromes. Future research should focus on RCTs that include a broader spectrum of older adults (≥75 years of age). Comprehensive assessments of frailty, cognitive function, and life expectancy should be integrated into revascularization guidelines. Developing tools for individualized decision-making that incorporate patient preferences, geriatric risks, and holistic care outcomes is essential for optimizing management. Proteomic and genomic profiling could enhance patient stratification by identifying biomarkers associated with aging, frailty, and cardiovascular risk. Moreover, there is a need for better pharmacologic approaches tailored to older adults, considering age-related changes in drug metabolism and increased polypharmacy risks. Enhanced shared decision-making frameworks that incorporate patient preferences, life expectancy, and personalized risk profiles are essential to guide optimal revascularization strategies for older adults. CONCLUSION The aging of the world population and the growing burden of CVD present unique challenges that demand specialized care for older adults undergoing revascularization. These patients with age-related physiologic changes, complex coronary anatomy, and prevalent geriatric syndromes require a nuanced and individualized approach to management. Coronary revascularization can offer benefits, such as symptom relief and improved outcomes, but the risks associated with invasive

CONCLUSION The aging of the world population and the growing burden of CVD present unique challenges that demand specialized care for older adults undergoing revascularization. These patients with age-related physiologic changes, complex coronary anatomy, and prevalent geriatric syndromes require a nuanced and individualized approach to management. Coronary revascularization can offer benefits, such as symptom relief and improved outcomes, but the risks associated with invasive procedures necessitate careful consideration of clinical status, frailty, and personal goals. Future research should aim to close knowledge gaps by including diverse older adults in clinical trials, using proteomic and genomic profiling for better risk stratification, and advancing decision-making frameworks that emphasize personalized care.

The 2023 ESC focused update of the 2021 HF guidelines introduced new key recommendations based on the results of the last years of science. First, two drugs, sodium– glucose co-transporter-2 (SGLT2) inhibitors and ﬁnerenone, a novel nonsteroidal, selective mineralocorticoid receptor antag- onist (MRA), are recommended for the prevention of HF in patients with diabetic chronic kidney disease (CKD). Second, SGLT2 inhibitors are now recommended for the treatment of HF across the entire left ventricular ejection fraction spectrum. The beneﬁts of quadruple therapy in patients with HF with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) are well established. Its rapid and early up-titration along with a close follow-up with frequent clinical and laboratory re-assessment after an episode of acute HF (the so-called ‘high-intensity care’ strategy) was associated with better outcomes in the STRONG-HF trial. Patients experiencing an episode of worsening HF might require a ﬁfth drug, vericiguat. In the STEP-HFpEF-DM and STEP-HFpEF trials, semaglutide 2.4 mg once weekly administered for 1 year decreased body weight and signiﬁcantly improved quality of life and the 6 min walk distance in obese patients with HF with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) with or without a history of dia- betes. Further data on safety and efﬁcacy, including also hard endpoints, are needed to support the addition of acetazolamide or hydrochlorothiazide to a standard diuretic regimen in patients hospitalized due to acute HF. In the meantime, PUSH-AHF supported the use of natriuresis-guided diuretic therapy. Further options and most recent evidence for the treatment of HF, including speciﬁc drugs for cardiomyopathies (i.e., mavacamten in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and tafamidis in transthyretin cardiac amyloidosis), device therapies, cardiac contractility modulation and percutaneous treatment of valvulopathies, with the recent ﬁnding from the TRILUMINATE Pivotal trial, are also reviewed in this article. documents.title: 2023 ACC expert consensus on tricuspid regurgitation

chunks.content: 1. Introduction The continual development of cardiac surgery has benefited many patients with left-sided valve diseases. Some patients would have tricuspid regurgitation (TR) late after left-sided valve surgery (LSVS) during long-term follow-up. Isolated tricuspid regurgitation after left-sided valve surgery (iTR-LSVS) refers to isolated TR without significant lesions in the mitral and/or aortic position late after mitral and/or aortic replacement or repair. Severe TR can lead to right heart failure, liver and renal dysfunction, and systemic congestion and has a negative impact on long-term prognosis. There is no clear recommendation on when and how intervention should be performed for patients with iTR-LSVS in the current guidelines for the management of valvular heart disease [ , , , ]. The operative mortality of isolated tricuspid valve surgery (iTVS) was historically as high as 10% [ , , , , , , , , ]. Minimally invasive techniques may reduce the operative mortality and complication rates despite lack of high-quality data [ , , , , , , , , ]. Recently, transcatheter tricuspid valve repair or replacement is becoming an alternative for selected patients [ , ]. To further understand iTR-LSVS, standardize the treatment, improve the prognosis, and promote the collaboration, the Chinese Minimally Invasive Cardiovascular Surgery Committee (CMICS) wrote this expert consensus. 2. Etiology The tricuspid valve has been disregarded for a long time because TR is usually secondary to left-sided valve disease rather than primary lesion. It was widely believed that treatment of left-sided valve diseases would lead to spontaneous resolution of TR, but increasing evidence has shown that TR in some patients may remain or even worsen late after LSVS. The pathogenesis of iTR-LSVS is complex and still not completely clear [ ]. The potential underlying mechanisms include the following: (1) The effective orifice area of the left-sided prosthetic valve or ring is too small, which leads to relative valve stenosis, increased left atrial pressure, pulmonary hypertension, right ventricle (RV) dilation, and functional TR [ ]. (2) Persistent atrial fibrillation causes dilation of the right atrium (RA) and tricuspid annulus [ ]. (3) The rheumatic lesion involves tricuspid leaflets, which results in thickening, contracture and fusion of leaflets and organic TR [ ]. (4) Mild or moderate TR is left untreated during prior LSVS or tricuspid repair without using annuloplasty rings [ ]. (5) The pacemaker lead passes through the tricuspid valve and causes TR [ ]. (6) Concomitant coronary artery disease may have a role in the development of TR [ ]. Given these possible underlying mechanisms of late TR, there are some recommendations for LSVS: (1) Valve repair should be the first choice if possible. (2) Use prosthetic valve as large as possible. (3) Tricuspid valve repair should be considered in patients with mild or moderate TR and a dilated annulus during LSVS. (4) Concomitant surgical ablation is recommended in patients with atrial fibrillation. 3. Preoperative Evaluation Transthoracic echocardiography is recommended to assess the severity of TR, the size and function of the RA and RV, and pulmonary artery pressure [ ]. A new TR grading scheme is recommended (Table ) [ , , , , ]. The vena contracta width (VCW) should be measured from the parasternal four-chamber and parasternal RV inflow views and then averaged [ ]. Velocity correction is recommended for two-dimensional proximal isovelocity surface area (PISA) measurement. The correction coefficient is V TRpeak /( V TRpeak – Va), in which Va is the aliasing velocity and V TRpeak is the peak velocity of TR [ ]. The three-dimensional PISA method does not require velocity correction [ ]. The systolic function of the RV in the longitudinal direction usually decreases after cardiac surgery with compensation by the radial direction [ ]. Accurate evaluation of the RV systolic function with any single index is difficult [ , ]. Therefore, measurement of both tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion (TAPSE) and right ventricular fractional area change (FAC) is preferred. When TAPSE is less than 16 mm and/or FAC is less than 35%, systolic dysfunction of the RV is indicated. Right heart catheterization is a critical method for evaluating RV function, which can accurately measure RA and RV pressure, pulmonary artery pressure, pulmonary capillary wedge pressure, cardiac output and cardiac index. It is recommended to perform right heart catheterization preoperatively if available, especially for patients with poor RV function and severe pulmonary artery hypertension. Cardiac output, cardiac index and RV diastolic pressure reflect RV function. Pulmonary vascular resistance reflects RV afterload. Pulmonary capillary wedge pressure indicates left atrial pressure. It is worth noting that there is certain discordance in pulmonary artery pressure estimated by echocardiography and right heart catheterization in severe TR, as the former tends to underestimate or overestimate pulmonary artery pressure [ ]. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging may be helpful for measurement of RV volume and

and cardiac index. It is recommended to perform right heart catheterization preoperatively if available, especially for patients with poor RV function and severe pulmonary artery hypertension. Cardiac output, cardiac index and RV diastolic pressure reflect RV function. Pulmonary vascular resistance reflects RV afterload. Pulmonary capillary wedge pressure indicates left atrial pressure. It is worth noting that there is certain discordance in pulmonary artery pressure estimated by echocardiography and right heart catheterization in severe TR, as the former tends to underestimate or overestimate pulmonary artery pressure [ ]. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging may be helpful for measurement of RV volume and function. Tests of liver and renal function, coagulation function and complete blood count are also necessary. When pulmonary capillary wedge pressure is higher than 15 mmHg, the function of the left-sided valves should be assessed. It is recommended to consider the necessity of concomitant surgery for the left-sided valves based on the patient’s status if the following conditions occur. In the mitral position, (1) the effective orifice area is less than 2 cm 2 due to pannus on the prosthetic valve or mobility disorders of the prosthetic leaflets or (2) moderate or severe mitral regurgitation or paravalvular leak exist. In the aortic position, severe prosthetic valve stenosis or regurgitation exists. Preoperative risk stratification is critical for patient selection. The Society of Thoracic Surgeons (STS) score and the EuroSCORE II are not suitable for iTVS. A few models are dedicated to iTVS, such as the Clinical Risk Score, TRI-SCORE, and MELD Score [ , , ]. However, patients with TR are highly heterogeneous, and different etiologies determine different prognoses [ , , , , ]. iTR-LSVS is more common in China than in Western countries and has a relatively poor prognosis among different kinds of TR [ ]. The value of the abovementioned models for iTR-LSVS is still unclear. A thorough preoperative assessment is necessary for each patient, and a specific risk scoring model for iTR-LSVS should be built [ , ]. 4. Indications for Intervention Based on recent studies, intervention is recommended for patients with the following conditions. (1) Severe TR. (2) Normal left ventricular function with ejection fraction ≥ 50%. (3) Symptoms of right heart failure, such as ascites, peripheral edema, pleural effusions, and poor appetite, or asymptomatic or mild symptoms but progressive right heart dilatation and dysfunction. Any following conditions should be considered high-risk. (1) Severe RV dysfunction, that is, TAPSE less than 10 mm or FAC less than 25%. (2) Pulmonary artery systolic pressure greater than 60 mmHg or pulmonary vascular resistance greater than 4 wood units. (3) Liver cirrhosis or elevated blood ammonia. The timing of intervention is an important determinant of postoperative outcome. The current guidelines have no clear recommendation due to the lack of evidence [ , , , ]. One reason for the historically high mortality of iTVS after LSVS may be the delay in referral to surgery, which may lead to irreversible RV failure [ , , , , , ]. Thus, it is gradually accepted that early surgical correction should be performed before the development of irreversible RV dysfunction and end-organ damage, despite a lack of high-quality randomized controlled trials [ ]. 5. Surgical Treatment Repair or replacement : The severity of leaflet pathological lesions and tricuspid annulus dilation, right heart function, and the feasibility of repair should be taken into consideration when choosing the therapeutic strategy. Tricuspid valve repair (TVr) is preferred for patients with mild leaflet pathological lesions, and those who are expected to have favorable outcomes with reliable repair techniques. TVr techniques generally include annuloplasty with a prosthetic ring, leaflet patch augmentation, edge-to-edge, artificial chordae implantation, and other techniques [ ]. In contrast, tricuspid valve replacement (TVR) is likely to be suitable for patients with significant rheumatic damage in leaflets, those with severe leaflet tethering due to severe dilation of the RV and tricuspid annulus, and those who are likely to have uncertain outcomes even after complex repair techniques [ , ]. Long-term follow-up data are still required to compare the outcomes of TVr and TVR for patients with iTR-LSVS. Choice of prosthetic valve : For TVR, the selection of prosthetic valve is still controversial [ ]. The relevant meta-analyses showed that there are no significant differences between mechanical and bioprosthetic valves in terms of survival or reoperation rate after TVR [ , , , ]. Considering that mechanical valves in the tricuspid position have a higher risk of valve thrombosis and that patients with iTR-LSVS are usually elderly and fragile, bioprosthetic valves may be preferred when patients are aged > 60 years [ , ]. However, there is no clear recommendation about the age at which it is reasonable to use a bioprosthetic valve in the tricuspid position in the current American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association

relevant meta-analyses showed that there are no significant differences between mechanical and bioprosthetic valves in terms of survival or reoperation rate after TVR [ , , , ]. Considering that mechanical valves in the tricuspid position have a higher risk of valve thrombosis and that patients with iTR-LSVS are usually elderly and fragile, bioprosthetic valves may be preferred when patients are aged > 60 years [ , ]. However, there is no clear recommendation about the age at which it is reasonable to use a bioprosthetic valve in the tricuspid position in the current American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association (ACC/AHA) and European Society of Cardiology/European Association for Cardio-Thoracic Surgery (ESC/EACTS) guidelines [ , ]. With the development of the tricuspid valve-in-valve technique, bioprosthetic valves may be used in younger patients in the tricuspid position, but more data are still needed [ , ]. Surgical approach : For patients without obvious adhesions in the right thoracic cavity, it might be suitable for endoscopy-assisted or totally endoscopic surgery via a right minithoracotomy in the 4th intercostal space. A temporary pacemaker lead is recommended to be placed through the internal jugular vein preoperatively. The arterial cannula is inserted through the femoral artery with the Seldinger technique. The venous cannula is inserted through the femoral vein to the superior vena cava without dissection or ligation of the vena cava. The beating-heart technique is used without clamping the ascending aorta. Right atriotomy is performed directly through the pericardium without liberation of the RA. Vacuum-assisted femoral venous drainage, maintaining less than –40 mmHg negative pressure, can suck up most of the blood and ensure a clean operative view. The surgical field is filled with carbon dioxide at a flow of 0.5–1.0 L/min. For patients with obvious adhesions in the right thoracic cavity, median thoracotomy can be used. For patients who need concomitant left-sided valve reoperation, the surgical approach should be determined based on a comprehensive preoperative evaluation. 6. Transcatheter Therapy Various transcatheter tricuspid valve repair and replacement systems are undergoing preclinical or clinical trials, and their early safety and feasibility have been confirmed. The current transcatheter tricuspid valve repair devices include TriClip (Abbott Vascular, Santa Clara, CA, USA), PASCAL (Edwards Lifesciencies, Irvine, CA, USA), FORMA (Edwards Lifesciencies, Irvine, CA, USA), TriAlign (Mitralign, Tewksbury, MA, USA), Cardioband (Edwards Lifesciencies, Irvine, CA, USA), K-Clip (Huihe Medical Technology, Shanghai, China) and others [ , , , , , ]. The available transcatheter tricuspid valve replacement systems include NaviGate (NaviGate Cardiac Structures, Lake Forest, CA, USA), LuX-Valve (Jenscare Biotechnology, Ningbo, China), Evoque (Edwards Lifesciencies, Irvine, CA, USA) and others [ , , ]. Despite convincing evidences in the field of percutaneous treatment of TR are relatively limited, transcatheter therapy may provide additional benefits over medical therapy alone [ , ]. Recently, a randomized controlled trial demonstrated that transcatheter edge-to-edge repair was safe for patients with symptomatic severe tricuspid regurgitation, and the severity of tricuspid regurgitation was reduced to moderate or less at 1 year in the majority of patients [ ]. Although these studies did not focus on iTR-LSVS patients and long-term outcomes were lack, transcatheter therapy can be considered for iTR-LSVS patients with clinical symptoms, prohibitive or high risk for surgical treatment, and suitable anatomical conditions [ ]. 7. Postoperative Management One of the high-risk periods for RV failure is the early postoperative phase. The increased postoperative RV afterload, as well as perioperative hypoxemia, hypercapnia and acidosis, may aggravate RV failure. The clinical manifestations of RV failure include systemic hypotension, organ dysfunction, and elevated RV filling pressure. Patients might also suffer from acidosis and decreased mixed venous oxygen saturation, while the increases in pulmonary artery pressure and pulmonary capillary wedge pressure depend on the severity of left ventricular dysfunction or preoperative pulmonary hypertension. Determining the fluid responsiveness of the patient is the key to manage RV failure. For patients with cardiogenic shock and fluid overload, renal replacement therapy should be started early for “negative fluid resuscitation” [ ]. Norepinephrine or vasopressin is the first option to maintain blood pressure in patients with hypotension. Dobutamine or milrinone can also reduce RV afterload by dilating the pulmonary artery [ ]. Factors that might induce pulmonary hypertension should be avoided, and low-tidal-volume mechanical ventilation should be given insofar as oxygenation and ventilation conditions allow. Inhalation of nitric oxide is another effective therapy to reduce pulmonary vascular resistance for RV failure when conventional therapies are not effective [ , ]. Prostaglandin analogs, such as iloprost and prostacyclin, can also be adopted as adjunct treatments for intractable RV failure. 8. Conclusions TR worsens the long-term prognosis of patients with iTR-LSVS. The timing and methods of intervention are of utmost significance. It is generally accepted that intervention should be performed before irreversible RV failure occurs. For patients with mild tricuspid valve lesions and patients

low-tidal-volume mechanical ventilation should be given insofar as oxygenation and ventilation conditions allow. Inhalation of nitric oxide is another effective therapy to reduce pulmonary vascular resistance for RV failure when conventional therapies are not effective [ , ]. Prostaglandin analogs, such as iloprost and prostacyclin, can also be adopted as adjunct treatments for intractable RV failure. 8. Conclusions TR worsens the long-term prognosis of patients with iTR-LSVS. The timing and methods of intervention are of utmost significance. It is generally accepted that intervention should be performed before irreversible RV failure occurs. For patients with mild tricuspid valve lesions and patients who are expected to achieve favorable outcomes with reliable repair techniques, TVr is recommended. Otherwise, TVR may be a better choice. Minimally invasive techniques may reduce the operative mortality and complication rates. The evolving transcatheter tricuspid valve repair or replacement will become an alternative for selected patients with iTR-LSVS in the future. This expert consensus reflects the current state of the art and is designed to evolve with the field.

chunks.content: 1. Introduction Cardiovascular disease (CVD) has been, and continues to be, the leading cause of death worldwide. In 2022, it accounted for more than nine million deaths and was the primary contributor to years of life lost due to disability [ ]. Although age-adjusted mortality rates have declined over recent decades, population aging and demographic growth are driving a steady increase in the overall burden of CVD. Between 2025 and 2050, cardiovascular deaths are projected to rise by 73%, reaching 35 million annually, while the prevalence of CVD is expected to nearly double [ ] ( ). Moreover, a disproportionate impact is anticipated across regions, sexes, and socioeconomic levels, along with a sharp rise in healthcare costs, which could exceed $1.3 trillion annually in countries like the United States by 2050 [ ]. Among modifiable risk factors, dyslipidemia ranks as the second most relevant metabolic contributor to the prevention of CVD, following hypertension [ ]. The evidence is clear: elevated levels of low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDLc) cause atherosclerosis and increase the risk of cardiovascular events, making lipid control a major therapeutic priority [ ]. For decades, the management of dyslipidemia has been largely “LDL-centric”; however, in recent years, this approach has evolved rapidly with the emergence of new biomarkers, advanced therapies, and digital tools that enable more precise and personalized lipid management. A significant cardiovascular risk persists despite achieving optimal LDLc targets, a phenomenon known as residual risk [ ]. This has prompted the investigation of new biomarkers ( ) that enable more accurate risk assessment. Apolipoprotein B (ApoB), which reflects the total number of atherogenic particles, and non-high-density lipoprotein (non-HDLc) cholesterol have proven to be more robust predictors in certain contexts. In addition, other markers such as lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] and remnant particles, triglyceride-rich metabolic byproducts, have been independently associated with residual cardiovascular risk [ , ]. Moreover, oxidation of lipid particles, particularly LDLc, enhances their atherogenic potential. The measurement of oxidized LDLc has been linked to greater atherosclerotic progression and a higher incidence of cardiovascular events, even among patients treated with statins [ ]. The development of new diagnostic tools has significantly expanded our ability to characterize the lipid profile and its clinical implications. Computed tomography (CT) enables quantification of coronary artery calcium as well as epicardial fat, an emerging marker of atherosclerosis associated with local inflammation [ ]. Techniques such as magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS) and mass spectrometry allow for highly precise analysis of the number, size, and composition of lipoprotein particles [ ]. Lipidomics, based on these platforms, has identified multiple lipid species associated with the progression of atherosclerosis and cardiovascular events. This data can be integrated with other multi-omic panels through machine learning algorithms capable of handling high-dimensional datasets. This strategy has been shown to improve cardiovascular risk prediction and re-stratification with greater accuracy and personalization compared to traditional clinical models [ ]. The digital revolution and the rise of personalized medicine have also driven the adoption of wearable devices, mobile applications, and artificial intelligence (AI) algorithms that support continuous monitoring and early risk stratification, allowing for the identification of individualized risk profiles at earlier stages [ ]. Technological advances have also had a major impact on the therapeutic landscape, with the emergence of new molecules such as PCSK9 inhibitors and RNA-based therapies, which have expanded treatment options and enabled better lipid control with more convenient dosing regimens [ ]. Additionally, technologies such as gene editing (CRISPR-Cas9) and therapeutic nanotechnology are emerging as disruptive strategies for the treatment of hereditary dyslipidemias and forms resistant to conventional therapies [ ]. This document presents a critical review of the most relevant advances in the diagnosis, monitoring, and treatment of dyslipidemia, with a particular focus on the integration of new technologies. The aim is to provide a comprehensive overview of the current state and future perspectives at the intersection of lipidology and technology, within the framework of precision medicine. 2. Methods A narrative literature review was conducted to explore the most recent and relevant advances in technologies applied to lipidology. The review included original research articles, clinical trials, meta-analyses, and systematic reviews published until May 2025. A structured search was performed using PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase Scopus, SciELO and Web of Science databases with combinations of the following keywords: “cholesterol”, “low-density lipoprotein”, “high-density lipoprotein”, “lipoprotein a”, “lipidomics”, “lipoproteins”, “lipid biomarkers”, “wearable devices”, “biosensors”, “telemedicine”, “RNA therapies”, “PCSK9 inhibitors”, “CRISPR-Cas9”, “nanotechnology”, “artificial intelligence”, “deep learning”, “neural network”, and “machine learning”. Preprints were considered only if they presented significant or pioneering findings. Eligibility was determined based on relevance to the integration of novel technologies in lipid management, including diagnostic tools, treatment modalities, and digital health applications. The selected studies were critically appraised and grouped into thematic domains reflecting the structure of this review: advanced lipid profiling, diagnostic devices, remote monitoring technologies, emerging therapies,

Science databases with combinations of the following keywords: “cholesterol”, “low-density lipoprotein”, “high-density lipoprotein”, “lipoprotein a”, “lipidomics”, “lipoproteins”, “lipid biomarkers”, “wearable devices”, “biosensors”, “telemedicine”, “RNA therapies”, “PCSK9 inhibitors”, “CRISPR-Cas9”, “nanotechnology”, “artificial intelligence”, “deep learning”, “neural network”, and “machine learning”. Preprints were considered only if they presented significant or pioneering findings. Eligibility was determined based on relevance to the integration of novel technologies in lipid management, including diagnostic tools, treatment modalities, and digital health applications. The selected studies were critically appraised and grouped into thematic domains reflecting the structure of this review: advanced lipid profiling, diagnostic devices, remote monitoring technologies, emerging therapies, artificial intelligence applications, and clinical decision support systems. Reference lists of included articles and recent reviews were manually screened to identify additional pertinent studies. 3. Advances in Lipid Profiling Atherosclerosis is the underlying mechanism of vascular disease development, and its relationship with lipoproteins is well recognized. Traditionally, cardiovascular risk assessment and treatment decisions have relied on standard plasma lipid measurements such as total cholesterol (TC), LDLc, HDLc, and triglycerides. However, achieving therapeutic targets has not been sufficient for avoiding recurrent vascular events. This is probably related to the inability of these conventional parameters to accurately estimate the individual atherogenic risk, particularly in patients with discordant lipid profiles or complex metabolic conditions. Consequently, advanced lipoprotein characterization has emerged as a promising tool to enhance cardiovascular risk stratification. Currently, a basic lipid profile must include not only the conventional measurements but also non-HDL cholesterol (determined by TC—HDLc) and apolipoprotein B determinations [ ]. Despite what was previously considered, LDLc levels are not the primary determinant for developing atherosclerotic vascular disease. In recent years, growing evidence has suggested that the retention of cholesterol-rich ApoB–containing lipoproteins within the arterial wall is closely associated with the incidence of vascular events [ ]. This relationship appears to be strongly influenced by both the number and size of these atherogenic particles [ ]. Several studies have demonstrated the utility of ApoB measurement as a surrogate for the number of atherogenic lipoprotein particles, since ApoB is present on all of them except HDLc. In contrast, non-HDL cholesterol provides an approximate estimate of the total cholesterol content within ApoB-containing lipoproteins. Both parameters offer complementary information and are strongly correlated [ ]. Furthermore, a once-in-a-lifetime Lp(a) determination should be considered to help stratify patients’ vascular risk. This is especially relevant in subjects with elevated Lp(a), since ApoB underestimates their vascular risk due to the increased atherogenicity of Lp(a) compared to that of LDLc [ ]. In recent years, there has been an unstoppable development in technology that has enabled us to go beyond blood lipid tests. Mass spectrometry has revolutionized the field of lipidomics by enabling the identification and quantification of thousands of lipid species based on charge, size, mass, and shape. The use of lipidomics can, hence, help identify new lipid biomarkers associated with CVD, potentially leading to early diagnosis. This technology can also be used to find new drug targets and map out lipid metabolic pathways involved in atherogenesis [ ]. Simultaneously, techniques such as nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy allow for the quantification of lipoprotein particle number and size, derived from the biological sample (serum or plasma) proton NMR spectrum of the patient. Each class of lipoproteins—LDLc, HDLc, and very low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (VLDLc)—emits a unique spectral line shape that allows them to be distinguished from one another. Regarding particle quantification, NMR signal amplitude is directly proportional to the number of particles emitting the signal [ ]. As we highlighted before, particle size and number may be stronger predictors of vascular risk than traditional lipid measures. Therefore, incorporating these advanced techniques into risk stratification is essential to identify individuals with elevated residual risk who may benefit from more intensive therapeutic interventions. 4. Novel Devices and Telemedicine in Lipidology The development of diagnostic and monitoring technologies has significantly transformed the way cardiovascular and metabolic diseases are detected, managed, and prevented. In particular, the emergence of portable, digital, and connected tools has enabled the decentralization of risk factor management by facilitating their monitoring outside the hospital setting and promoting greater patient autonomy. In this context, innovative devices have emerged that can measure biochemical parameters, record physiological data, and support clinical decision-making through integrated systems. Among the most relevant current strategies are electrochemical sensors capable of quantifying cholesterol levels from a small blood sample ( ) [ ]. These are generally classified into two main categories based on their detection principle: - Enzymatic sensors: the most established technology, employing enzymes such as cholesterol oxidase (ChOx) and cholesterol esterase (ChE). These devices, found in commercial products like CardioCheck ® Plus (PTS Diagnostics, Indianapolis, IN, USA) and Accutrend ® Plus (Roche Diagnostics, Mannheim, Germany), enable rapid measurement of total cholesterol, HDLc, LDLc, and triglycerides from a drop of capillary blood. Although they

clinical decision-making through integrated systems. Among the most relevant current strategies are electrochemical sensors capable of quantifying cholesterol levels from a small blood sample ( ) [ ]. These are generally classified into two main categories based on their detection principle: - Enzymatic sensors: the most established technology, employing enzymes such as cholesterol oxidase (ChOx) and cholesterol esterase (ChE). These devices, found in commercial products like CardioCheck ® Plus (PTS Diagnostics, Indianapolis, IN, USA) and Accutrend ® Plus (Roche Diagnostics, Mannheim, Germany), enable rapid measurement of total cholesterol, HDLc, LDLc, and triglycerides from a drop of capillary blood. Although they offer high sensitivity and specificity, their performance can be affected by the instability of enzymes under environmental conditions (pH, temperature). Another limitation is their high cost. - Non-enzymatic sensors: currently under development, these systems rely on the direct oxidation of cholesterol on electrodes modified with nanomaterials such as graphene, metal oxides, or carbon nanotubes, offering greater robustness, stability, and lower potential cost. Both types of sensors have been integrated into miniaturized lab-on-a-chip (LoC) platforms, which can operate with minimal sample volumes (microliters) and are suited for portable and multifunctional diagnostic settings. These devices incorporate microchannels for handling biological fluids and sensors that generate signals proportional to the concentration of the target analyte [ , ]. In addition, non-invasive devices such as skin patches and smart contact lenses with integrated optical biosensors have been developed to detect cholesterol in sweat and tears, respectively, with promising results in preclinical studies [ ]. In parallel, mobile biosensors integrated with smartphones are being evaluated. These use colorimetric or chemiluminescent systems for cholesterol detection. In the case of colorimetric sensors, paper strips functionalized with enzymes react with the sample, producing a color change that can be quantified using the phone’s camera. Chemiluminescent sensors, on the other hand, involve chemical reactions that emit light upon interaction with cholesterol in biological samples; this light is also detected by the smartphone camera, usually under controlled conditions (using dark boxes and optical filters). Although still in the experimental phase, these technologies represent an accessible, cost-effective, and adaptable approach to self-monitoring and home-based lipid assessment, especially in low-resource settings [ ]. In recent years, the growing use of wearable devices (such as smartwatches) and mobile health (mHealth) apps has opened new avenues for monitoring cardiometabolic risk. While these tools do not measure lipid levels directly, they allow for tracking of relevant physiological parameters such as heart rate, blood pressure, sleep, and physical activity. When integrated into digital platforms, these data contribute to overall risk estimation and improve adherence to lifestyle interventions [ ]. In fact, some studies have shown significant reductions in LDL cholesterol using health apps combined with nutritional strategies and structured physical activity programs [ ]. The added value of these technologies lies in their ability to integrate with digital health programs and telemedicine platforms, enabling continuous, personalized, and proactive monitoring of patients with dyslipidemia or at risk of developing it. Telemedicine has gained increasing relevance in this area by facilitating continuity of care without requiring in-person visits. Digital health platforms allow healthcare professionals to access clinical data, lab results, and records from portable devices, optimizing real-time decision-making. This model has proven particularly useful during events such as the COVID-19 pandemic and in rural areas with limited healthcare access. Several recent studies have demonstrated the effectiveness of remote care programs in managing cardiovascular risk factors. For example, Blood et al. implemented a remote management program for over 10,000 patients, combining automated algorithms, laboratory monitoring, and virtual consultations to control hypertension and dyslipidemia, achieving significant clinical improvements in diverse populations [ ]. Likewise, Choi et al. reported improvements in lipid profiles and postprandial glycemic control in patients with type-2 diabetes through telemonitoring strategies [ ]. The integration of data from personal devices, mobile apps, and periodic biochemical testing into telemedicine platforms provides a comprehensive view of cardiometabolic risk, enhancing therapeutic adherence, clinical control, and healthcare system efficiency ( ). In this regard, remote care is emerging as a strategic pillar in the long-term follow-up of patients with dyslipidemia and the implementation of evidence-based preventive interventions. 5. Emerging Lipid-Lowering Therapies Oral lipid-lowering therapies include statins, ezetimibe, and, more recently, bempedoic acid. Despite all of them having demonstrated in clinical trials to significantly reduce the risk of cardiovascular outcomes in patients with dyslipidemia, the fact is that LDLc control rates remain far from optimal [ , , ]. This is due to an underuse of lipid-lowering therapies, including PCSK9 inhibitors, but also because new drugs with complementary mechanisms of action are warranted [ , ]. Emerging pharmacological therapies are transforming lipid management, enabling a more targeted and precise approach. Currently, agents such as PCSK9 inhibitors (monoclonal antibodies) and inclisiran (a small interfering ribonucleic acid [siRNA]) are routinely integrated into clinical practice
